Combining DES with the baseline Planck likelihood pulls the Planck result to lower Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} and slightly lower σ8\sigma_{8}, giving

S8=0.811±0.011,Ωm=0.3040±0.0060,σ8=0.8062±0.0057,}68 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+DES.\left.\begin{aligned} S_{8}&=0.811\pm 0.011,\\ \Omega_{\mathrm{m}}&=0.3040\pm 0.0060,\\ \sigma_{8}&=0.8062\pm 0.0057,\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{113.81102pt}{\begin{flushleft}68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+{DES}. \end{flushleft}}}} (31)

A similar shift is seen without including Planck lensing, and is disfavoured by Planck CMB with a total Δ​χeff2≈13\Delta\chi^{2}_{\rm eff}\approx 13 for the CMB likelihoods (comparing the Planck-only best fit to the fit when combined with DES). The shift in parameters is also larger than would be expected for Gaussian distributions, given the small change in parameter covariance. The corresponding change in χeff2\chi^{2}_{\rm eff} for the DES likelihood is Δ​χeff2≈10\Delta\chi^{2}_{\rm eff}\approx 10, which is high, but less surprising given the 4​–​54\text{--}5 contribution expected from the number of parameters that are much better constrained by Planck. The summary consistency statistic χeff,joint2−χeff,DES2−χeff,Planck2≈14\chi^{2}_{\rm eff,joint}-\chi^{2}_{\rm eff,DES}-\chi^{2}_{\rm eff,Planck}\approx 14, which is high at the roughly 1%1\thinspace\% PTE level, given the expected value of 4, assuming roughly Gaussian statistics (Raveri & Hu 2019).

In summary, the DES combined probes of Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} parameters are in moderate percent-level tension with Planck. Whether this is a statistical fluctuation, evidence for systematics, or new physics is currently unclear. In this paper, we follow the philosophy of 276 and 284 of making minimal use of other astrophysical data in combination with Planck, using BAO as our primary complementary data set. We therefore do not include DES results in most of the parameter constraints discussed in this paper. We do, however, consider the impact of the DES weak lensing results on dark-energy and modified-gravity constraints in Sect. 7.4 and on neutrino masses in Sect. 7.5.1. We also include DES for a wider range of models in the Planck parameter tables available on the 273.

5.7 Cluster counts

Counts of clusters of galaxies provide an additional way of constraining the amplitude of the power spectrum at low redshifts (e.g., Pierpaoli et al. 2001; Komatsu & Seljak 2002, and references therein). Planck clusters, selected via the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich (tSZ) signature, were used to explore cosmological parameters in Planck Collaboration XX (2014). This analysis was revisited using a deeper sample of Planck clusters in Planck Collaboration XXIV (2016). We have not produced a new tSZ cluster catalogue in the 2018 Planck data release and so the results presented in this section are based on the 439 clusters in the MMF3 cluster cosmology sample, as analysed in Planck Collaboration XXIV (2016). Comparison with the 2018 CMB Planck power spectrum results show differences primarily from changes to the base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model parameters caused by the tighter constraints on τ\tau. The impact of the lower value of τ\tau reported in Planck Collaboration Int. XLVI (2016) on the interpretation of cluster counts has been discussed by Salvati et al. (2018).

We first review the main results from Planck Collaboration XXIV (2016). There has been increasing recognition that the calibration of cluster masses is the dominant uncertainty in using cluster counts to estimate cosmological parameters. In the analysis of Planck clusters, the cluster tSZ observable was related to the cluster mass M500M_{500}2626 26 The mass contained within a sphere of radius R500R_{500}, centred on the cluster, where R500R_{500} is the radius at which the mean density is 500 times the critical density at the redshift of the cluster. using X-ray scaling relations (Arnaud et al. 2010), calibrated against a subsample of the Planck clusters. The X-ray masses are, however, derived assuming hydrostatic equilibrium and are expected to be biased low (Nagai et al. 2007, e.g.,). This was accounted for by multiplying the true masses by a so-called “hydrostatic mass bias” factor of (1−b)(1-b). The strongest constraints on this bias factor come from weak gravitational lensing estimates of cluster masses. Planck Collaboration XXIV (2016) considered three lensing mass calibrations2727 27 See Sifón et al. (2016) for a discussion of dynamical mass estimates for SZ-selected clusters.: (1−b)=0.69±0.07(1-b)=0.69\pm 0.07 from 22 Planck clusters from the Weighing the Giants lensing programme (von der Linden et al. 2014); (1−b)=0.78±0.08(1-b)=0.78\pm 0.08 from 37 Planck clusters calibrated by the Canadian Cluster Comparison Project (Hoekstra et al. 2015); and 1/(1−b)=0.99±0.191/(1-b)=0.99\pm 0.19 from Planck CMB-lensing mass estimates of the MMF3 cluster sample (Planck Collaboration XXIV 2016). More recently, Sereno et al. (2017) have analysed 35 Planck clusters with galaxy shear data from the CFHTLenS (Heymans et al. 2012) and RCSLenS (Hildebrandt et al. 2016) surveys, finding (1−b)≈0.77±0.11(1-b)\approx 0.77\pm 0.11 for all clusters and (1−b)=0.68±0.11(1-b)=0.68\pm 0.11 for the 15 clusters in the cosmological sample. Additionally, Penna-Lima et al. (2017) use gravitational lensing measurements from HST images of 21 Planck clusters finding (1−b)=0.73±0.10(1-b)=0.73\pm 0.10.

The determination of cosmological parameters such as σ8\sigma_{8} and Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} from Planck cluster counts is strongly dependent on the prior adopted for the mass bias parameter. In this paper, we use the Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing likelihood in combination with the Planck cluster counts to derive a constraint on (1−b)(1-b) (following similar analyses described in Planck Collaboration XX 2016 and Salvati et al. 2018). This gives

(32) is mainly caused by the 20182018 change in the τ\tau constraint. The mass bias of Eq. (32) is at the lower end of the weak-lensing mass estimates, but is about 2​σ2\thinspace\sigma lower that the Planck CMB-lensing mass calibration reported in Planck Collaboration XX (2016).

Zubeldia & Challinor (2019) have revisited the Planck CMB-lensing mass calibration, incorporating the CMB-lensing mass estimates within a likelihood describing the Planck cluster counts, together with a Planck prior on θMC\theta_{\rm MC}. This study corrects for significant biases in the analysis reported in Planck Collaboration XX (2016). Zubeldia & Challinor (2019) find (1−b)=0.71±0.10(1-b)=0.71\pm 0.10 and σ8​(Ωm/0.33)0.25=0.765±0.035\sigma_{8}(\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.33)^{0.25}=0.765\pm 0.035. Since 284 there have been a number of new analyses of cluster counts using other surveys. Two recent studies (Mantz et al. 2015; de Haan et al. 2016), with very different selection criteria, use weak gravitational lensing mass determinations from the Weighing the Giants programme to calibrate cluster scaling relations. de Haan et al. (2016) analysed a sample of 377 clusters at z>0.25z>0.25 identified with SPT, finding σ8​(Ωm/0.27)0.3=0.797±0.031\sigma_{8}(\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.27)^{0.3}=0.797\pm 0.031, while Mantz et al. (2015) analysed an X-ray-selected sample of clusters from the ROSAT All-Sky survey, finding σ8​(Ωm/0.3)0.17=0.81±0.03\sigma_{8}(\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.3)^{0.17}=0.81\pm 0.03. These measurements can be compared to our baseline Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} constraints (Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing) of σ8​(Ωm/0.27)0.3=0.849±0.010\sigma_{8}(\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.27)^{0.3}=0.849\pm 0.010 and σ8​(Ωm/0.3)0.17=0.817±0.076\sigma_{8}(\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.3)^{0.17}=0.817\pm 0.076.

Schellenberger & Reiprich (2017) have analysed a sample of 64 of the brightest X-ray clusters using a prior on the hydrostatic mass bias from Biffi et al. (2016). These authors find Ωm=0.303±0.009\Omega_{\rm m}=0.303\pm 0.009, σ8=0.790−0.028+0.030\sigma_{8}=0.790^{+0.030}_{-0.028}, and S8=σ8​(Ωm/0.3)1/2=0.792±0.054S_{8}=\sigma_{8}(\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}/0.3)^{1/2}=0.792\pm 0.054. Each of these numbers is within about 1​σ1\thinspace\sigma of the Planck base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} best-fit cosmology reported in this paper. Finally, we mention the analysis of ROSAT-observed X-ray clusters carried out by Böhringer et al. (2014); Böhringer et al. (2017). These authors choose a central value for the hydrostatic mass bias of (1−b)=0.9(1-b)=0.9, although they allow for small variations in the slope (7%7\thinspace\%) and normalization (14%14\thinspace\%) of the X-ray luminosity-mass relation; they find constraints the σ8\sigma_{8}–Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} plane in tension with Planck at about 2.5​σ2.5\thinspace\sigma.

In summary, accurate calibrations of cluster masses are essential if cluster counts are to be used as cosmological probes. Given the uncertainties in these calibrations, we do not use cluster counts in our main parameter grid. Consistency of cluster counts with the best-fit Planck base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} cosmology requires hydrostatic mass biases (Eq. 32) that are at the lower end, but within about 1​σ1\thinspace\sigma of bias factors estimated from weak-lensing cluster masses. The combined Planck CMB-lensing and cluster-count analysis reported by Zubeldia & Challinor (2019) is in good agreement with the Planck base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} cosmology. At this time, there is no compelling evidence for a discrepancy between Planck-, SPT-, or X-ray-selected cluster counts and the base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model.

6 Internal consistency of 𝚲\boldsymbol{\Lambda}CDM model parameters

In this section we briefly discuss a couple of curious features of the Planck data that lead to moderate tensions in parameter consistency tests. We first discuss how parameters vary between high and low multipoles, and the relevant features in the power spectra that may be responsible for these shifts. We then discuss the related issue of how the full multipole range appears to prefer more lensing than predicted by Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} fits. We end this section with a discussion of systematic uncertainties.

6.1 Consistency of high and low multipoles

The Planck CMB temperature power spectrum shows a conspicuous dip over the multipole range 20≲ℓ≲3020\la\ell\la 30 compared to Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} fits, as can be seen in Fig. 1. This feature was first observed by WMAP (Bennett et al. 2003), and was discussed in detail in 276. Since it is detected consistently by both WMAP and Planck at multiple frequencies, it cannot plausibly be explained by an instrumental systematic or foreground. The large-scale Planck temperature map is signal dominated, so the dip feature is almost identical in this final release. 276 also noted an approximately 2.7​σ2.7\thinspace\sigma mismatch between the best-fit Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} cosmology and the amplitude of the measured temperature power spectrum at ℓ≤30\ell\leq 30. However, with the tighter optical depth constraints used in this paper and improvements in the high multipole likelihoods we find no strong evidence for an amplitude mismatch. The Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing best-fit Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model provides a good overall fit to the temperature multipoles at ℓ<30\ell<30 (χeff2≈23\chi^{2}_{\rm eff}\approx 23 for 28 data points), and because of the skewed χ2\chi^{2}-like distribution of the CMB spectrum estimators, it is expected that typically more than half of the data points are below the theoretical model values (see Fig. 1). The statistical significance of the dip feature is hard to quantify, since it was identified a posteriori, but 283 suggest a significance of about 2.8 % after maximizing over extremal ℓ\ell ranges found in simulations. This could be an indication of new physics at large scales, for example associated with a sharp feature in the inflationary potential (as considered by Peiris et al. 2003, and many subsequent researchers). Alternatively, it could just be a statistical fluctuation, which is our baseline assumption. However, since the dip is a relatively unusual fluctuation and it is near one end of the multipole range, it tends to pull cosmological parameters more than would be expected in typical realizations of a Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} cosmology. This needs to be borne in mind in assessing parameter shifts between low and high multipoles.

WMAP measured the CMB temperature fluctuations up to ℓ≈800\ell\approx 800 (Bennett et al. 2013). The higher-resolution data from Planck substantially increases the multipole range of the temperature power spectrum out to ℓ≈2500\ell\approx 2500. Cosmological parameters are therefore expected to shift (usually towards the truth) from the mean posterior values measured by WMAP, together with a reduction in the error bars. This is what is seen, with the Planck values of H0H_{0} and nsn_{\rm s} decreasing, and Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}} and Ωm​h2\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}h^{2} increasing, along with substantially smaller errors. However as noted in 276 the magnitudes of the shifts appear to be slightly larger than might be expected statistically, assuming the base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} cosmology. This stimulated additional work on the consistency of the Planck power spectra reported in 283 and to further investigations of the consistency of cosmological parameters measured from high and low multipoles from Planck (Addison et al. 2016; Planck Collaboration Int. LI 2017). As noted in the introduction, there is a very good agreement between Planck and WMAP temperature maps on the scales observed by WMAP (Planck Collaboration I 2016; Huang et al. 2018), but an inconsistency with high multipoles could indicate either new physics beyond Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, or the presence of some unidentified systematics associated with the Planck data and/or the foreground model. Planck Collaboration Int. LI (2017) find that although some cosmological parameters differ by more than 2​σ2\thinspace\sigma between ℓ<800\ell<800 and ℓ>800\ell>800, accounting for the multi-dimensional parameter space including correlations between parameters, the shifts are at the 10 % level and hence not especially unusual. Nonetheless, parameter shifts, particularly in the fluctuation amplitude and Hubble parameter (which are directly relevant for the Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}-comparison with external data, as discussed in Sect. 5) are worth a brief re-examination using the additional information provided by the Planck polarization spectra.

Constraints on cosmological parameters from power spectra at high multipoles require a foreground model. Previous studies have shown that results are not very sensitive to the specific assumptions that are made within the broad context of slowly varying foreground spectra expected on physical grounds (Addison et al. 2016; Planck Collaboration Int. LI 2017). In this section, we use the plik_lite Planck likelihood, described in detail in 293, which has the standard Plik foreground and nuisance parameters marginalized out without further assumptions on the cosmology.2828 28 We do not attempt to quantify likelihood modelling differences in this section, but a CamSpec-based likelihood gives slightly less tension between high and low multipoles (especially with polarization), associated with the weaker preference for AL>1A_{\rm L}>1, as discussed in more detail in Sect. 6.2. For standard model extensions plik_lite accurately reproduces results from the full Plik likelihood. It allows us to explore the high-ℓ\ell likelihood accounting for foreground uncertainties, but with the foregrounds constrained in a sensible way from their spectra over the full multipole range. We consider the multipole ranges ℓ≤801\ell\leq 801 and ℓ≥802\ell\geq 802 (corresponding to the boundary of one of the plik_lite bins), so that the low-multipole range is roughly comparable to WMAP and the two ranges have similar statistical power on most parameters. Results splitting at ℓ≈1000\ell\approx 1000 are similar, but with larger errors in the high multipole range.

Figure 21 shows a comparison of the high and low multipole ranges, both for temperature (lower triangle, as previously discussed by Addison et al. 2016 and Planck Collaboration Int. LI 2017), and new results for the combined temperature-polarization likelihood (upper triangle). Part of the difference between the low- and high-multipole ranges is caused by the large-scale temperature dip discussed above; if we exclude multipoles ℓ<30\ell<30 (unfilled grey contours), the contours from ℓ≤801\ell\leq 801 shift towards the area of consistency with the high multipoles. This could indicate that the low-multipole results have been pulled unusually far from the truth by the large-scale power spectrum dip; if so, the WMAP temperature results would also have been pulled at a similar (but not identical) level. The region of overlap of the high- and low-multipole parameter constraints is consistent with constraints from the nearly-independent combination of E​EEE polarization and lensing with a conservative Ωb​h2\Omega_{\mathrm{b}}h^{2} prior (green contours). This is consistent with a statistical fluctuation pulling the low and high multipoles in opposite directions, so that their intersection is closer to the truth if Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} is correct.

Figure 22 shows marginalized individual parameter constraints, and also a comparison with the results from the polarization likelihoods at high and low multipoles. The ℓ≥802\ell\geq 802 temperature results pull parameters to a region of higher matter density and fluctuation amplitude (and to lower nsn_{\rm s} and H0H_{0}) than the lower multipole range, and predict a CMB lensing amplitude parameter σ8​Ωm0.25=0.649±0.018\sigma_{8}\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}^{0.25}=0.649\pm 0.018. This is in tension with the CMB lensing-reconstruction measurement of σ8​Ωm0.25=0.589±0.020\sigma_{8}\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}^{0.25}=0.589\pm 0.020 at 2.2​σ2.2\thinspace\sigma (as pointed out by Addison et al. 2016 with 2015 data; also see the closely-related discussion in the next subsection). As shown in Fig. 22, combining the ℓ≥802\ell\geq 802 CMB likelihood with the lensing reconstruction, all parameter results move back towards the same region of parameter space as combining with ℓ≤801\ell\leq 801, consistent with the high-ℓ\ell temperature result having fluctuated high along the main degeneracy direction. As discussed in Sects. 2.3 and 3.3, the combined CMB power spectrum results over the full multipole range are consistent with the lensing likelihood.

It is also interesting to compare to parameter constraints from the CMB power spectrum multipoles ℓ≤801\ell\leq 801 combined with the lensing and BAO, which gives

H0=(67.85±0.52)​km​s−1​Mpc−1,σ8=0.8058±0.0063,Ωm=0.3081±0.0065.}68 %, TT,TE,EE [ℓ≤801]+lowE+lensing+BAO.\left.\begin{aligned} H_{0}&=(67.85\pm 0.52)\thinspace\penalty\ \text{km}\penalty\ \text{s}^{-1}\text{Mpc}^{-1},\\ \sigma_{8}&=0.8058\pm 0.0063,\\ \Omega_{\mathrm{m}}&=0.3081\pm 0.0065.\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{71.13188pt}{\begin{flushleft}68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE [$\ell\leq 801$]\allowbreak+{lowE}\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO. \end{flushleft}}}} (33)

These results are entirely independent of the cosmological parameter fit to the ℓ≥801\ell\geq 801 power spectra, but agree well at the 1​σ1\thinspace\sigma level with the full joint results in Table 1 (which have similar errors on these parameters). An equivalent result could be obtained using WMAP data after replacing their low-ℓ\ell polarization with the Planck HFI measurement (i.e., lowE).

For the temperature likelihoods, the difference between the low- and high-multipole constraints remains evident, with Ωm​h2\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}h^{2} differing at the 2.8​σ2.8\thinspace\sigma level. Adding polarization, the results from the multipole ranges are more consistent, as shown in Fig. 22, though the difference in Ωm​h2\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}h^{2} is still unusual at the roughly 2​σ2\thinspace\sigma level. However, the shifts in the different parameters are all highly correlated, due to partial parameter degeneracies, so the significance of any individual large shift is lower after accounting for the number of parameters (Planck Collaboration Int. LI 2017). The internal tensions between multipole ranges appear to be consistent with moderate statistical fluctuations, related to the low-ℓ\ell dip at large scales and correlated with the lensing amplitude on small scales. The large-scale feature is well determined by both WMAP and Planck and very robustly measured. The internal consistency of the Planck power spectra between different frequencies and detectors (283, 293) argues against systematics driving large parameter shifts at high multipoles. Equation (33) also demonstrates that any effect from the high-multipole spectra alone cannot be pulling our baseline parameters by more than about 1​σ1\thinspace\sigma. In the next subsection we describe in more detail the apparent preference for a higher lensing amplitude, and the features in the observed spectrum that could be responsible for it.

6.2 Lensing smoothing and ALA_{\rm L}

In addition to the direct measurement of CMB lensing described in Sect. 2.3 and 294, lensing can be seen in the Planck CMB power spectra via the lensing-induced smoothing of the acoustic peaks and transfer of power to the damping tail. This effect is modelled in our main parameter analysis, and can be calculated accurately from the unlensed CMB power spectra and the CMB lensing potential power spectrum in each model (Seljak 1996; Lewis & Challinor 2006). Interesting consistency checks include testing if the amplitude of the smoothing effect in the CMB power matches expectation and whether the amplitude of the smoothing is consistent with that measured by the lensing reconstruction. To do this, the theoretical prediction for the lensing spectrum in each model is often scaled by an “ALA_{\rm L}” consistency parameter, where the theoretical expectation is that AL=1A_{\rm L}=1 (Calabrese et al. 2008).

As shown in Fig. 3, the Planck lensing-reconstruction power spectrum is consistent with the amplitude expected for Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} models that fit the CMB spectra, so the Planck lensing measurement is compatible with AL=1A_{\rm L}=1. However, the distributions of ALA_{\rm L} inferred from the CMB power spectra alone are shown in Fig. 23 for various different data combinations, and these indicate a preference for AL>1A_{\rm L}>1, with

AL\displaystyle A_{\rm L} =\displaystyle= 1.243±0.096(68%,Planck TT+lowE),\displaystyle 1.243\pm 0.096\quad(68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ \text{{Planck}\ TT\allowbreak+lowE}), (34a)
AL\displaystyle A_{\rm L} =\displaystyle= 1.180±0.065(68%,Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE),\displaystyle 1.180\pm 0.065\quad(68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ \text{{Planck}\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE}), (34b)

assuming a Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}+ALA_{\rm L} model. The TE polarization data alone slightly prefer AL<1A_{\rm L}<1, with the EE data slightly preferring AL>1A_{\rm L}>1; however, both are consistent with AL=1A_{\rm L}=1 within 2​σ2\thinspace\sigma. The joint combined likelihood shifts the value preferred by the TT data downwards towards AL=1A_{\rm L}=1, but the error also shrinks, increasing the significance of AL>1A_{\rm L}>1 to 2.8​σ2.8\thinspace\sigma (99.8%99.8\thinspace\% of parameter samples have AL>0A_{\rm L}>0, so the one-tailed limit is almost exactly 3​σ3\thinspace\sigma). Moreover, combining with the lensing likelihood further pulls the constraint towards AL=1A_{\rm L}=1, which is then consistent with the data to within 2​σ2\thinspace\sigma; we see that the preference for AL>1A_{\rm L}>1 is driven by the CMB power spectra alone.

The preference for high ALA_{\rm L} is not just a volume effect in the full parameter space (see 276 for discussion of such effects in multi-parameter fitting), with the best fit improved by Δ​χeff2=−8.7\Delta\chi^{2}_{\rm eff}=-8.7 when adding ALA_{\rm L} for TT+lowE and Δ​χeff2=−9.7\Delta\chi^{2}_{\rm eff}=-9.7 for TT,TE,EE+lowE. The bulk of the Δ​χeff2\Delta\chi^{2}_{\rm eff} comes from the high-ℓ\ell likelihood (mostly in the range 600<ℓ<1500600<\ell<1500); however, the low-ℓ\ell temperature commander likelihood fit is also improved if ALA_{\rm L} is free, with Δ​χeff2=−2.3\Delta\chi^{2}_{\rm eff}=-2.3 and Δ​χeff2=−1.3\Delta\chi^{2}_{\rm eff}=-1.3 for the TT+lowE and TT,TE,EE+lowE, respectively, due to the lower amplitude of the ALA_{\rm L} fit on large scales. The change in fit to the low-ℓ\ell polarization is not very significant (Δ​χeff2=−0.2\Delta\chi^{2}_{\rm eff}=-0.2 and Δ​χeff2=−0.4\Delta\chi^{2}_{\rm eff}=-0.4).

The determination of ALA_{\rm L} from the high-ℓ\ell polarization data and the TT,TE,EE+lowE joint combination depends on the calibration of the polarization channels, and is affected by different ways of modelling the polarization efficiencies, as discussed in Sect. 2.2. The results from the CamSpec likelihood (which uses spectrum-based rather than map-based calibrations for T​ETE and E​EEE) are somewhat shifted with respect to the Plik likelihood, as shown by the dotted lines in Fig. 23, and have larger errors, giving

AL\displaystyle A_{\rm L}\hskip-2.84526pt =\displaystyle= 1.246−0.100+0.092(68%,TT+lowE [CamSpec]),\displaystyle\hskip-2.84526pt1.246^{+0.092}_{-0.100}\quad(68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ \text{TT\allowbreak+lowE\penalty\ [{\tt CamSpec}]}), (35a)
AL\displaystyle A_{\rm L}\hskip-2.84526pt =\displaystyle= 1.149±0.072​(68%,TT,TE,EE+lowE [CamSpec]).\displaystyle\hskip-2.84526pt1.149\pm 0.072\ (68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ \text{TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\penalty\ [{\tt CamSpec}]}). (35b)

Using CamSpec there is still a clear preference for AL>1A_{\rm L}>1, but the joint result with polarization is now only just over 2​σ2\thinspace\sigma above AL=1A_{\rm L}=1. The differences between these Plik and CamSpec results arise from differences in the methodologies used to create the likelihoods. Although both likelihoods clearly show a preference for AL>1A_{\rm L}>1, this cannot be claimed to be a robust detection at much over 2​σ2\thinspace\sigma (Efstathiou & Gratton 2019, see also).

The preference for AL>1A_{\rm L}>1 within the Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model is a curious feature of the Planck CMB power spectrum data, and has already been discussed extensively in 276, 284, and Planck Collaboration Int. LI (2017), although it is now slightly more significant. In temperature, over half of the small (approximately 0.02) upward shift in ALA_{\rm L} compared to 2015 is explained by the lower optical depth from the 2018 low-ℓ\ell likelihood: lower τ\tau implies lower AsA_{\rm s} to match the high-ℓ\ell CMB fluctuation amplitude, and hence larger ALA_{\rm L} to yield a lensing amplitude and hence amount of smoothing at the same level as 2015. In polarization about 40%40\thinspace\% of the shift in ALA_{\rm L} is explained by changes in τ\tau, with changes in the maps, modelling for beam leakage, and polarization efficiencies explaining the rest.

The high-ℓ\ell temperature likelihood preference for more lensing smoothing than allowed by Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} can be seen by eye in the smoothed data residuals plotted in Fig. 24; over almost all the allowed Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} parameter space there is an oscillatory residual in the range 1100≲ℓ≲20001100\la\ell\la 2000 that matches the shape of the lensing smoothing2929 29 Although the oscillatory pattern looks most similar to lensing at high multipoles, an increase in the foreground model amplitude can decrease the oscillation amplitude in the theory contribution to the spectrum, and hence appear as an oscillatory difference. For example Δ​ns≈−0.02\Delta n_{\rm s}\approx-0.02, combined with an implausibly large change in the foreground model, gives a difference in the predicted spectrum with an oscillatory component that has similar amplitude to Δ​AL≈0.1\Delta A_{\rm L}\approx 0.1; see the related discussion in Planck Collaboration Int. LI (2017). (although in other multipole ranges it does not match at all). The residual is not obviously anomalous, with the TT Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} best fit improving by Δ​χ2≈4\Delta\chi^{2}\approx 4 if a best-fit oscillatory residual (with AL≈1.1A_{\rm L}\approx 1.1) is added to the best-fit Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} theory model. The stronger preference for AL>1A_{\rm L}>1 when ALA_{\rm L} varies arises because degeneracies between ALA_{\rm L}, cosmological parameters, and foregrounds improves the fit at both high and lower multipoles, as shown by the black dashed line in Fig. 24. In Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} the lensing amplitude can be increased by increasing Ωm​h2\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}h^{2}; however, the model then becomes a bad fit because of the poorer agreement at ℓ<1000\ell<1000). Varying ALA_{\rm L} allows a high ALA_{\rm L} to remove the oscillatory residual at high multipoles that appears in Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} with lower Ωm​h2\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}h^{2}, giving best fits with lower Ωm​h2\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}h^{2} and higher H0H_{0} (by 1.51.5–2.0​σ2.0\thinspace\sigma, depending on the exact combination of data used) that are not favoured in the physical Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model. Lower values of Ωm​h2\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}h^{2} give higher values of nsn_{\rm s}, lowering the theory prediction on large scales, so high ALA_{\rm L} models are also slightly preferred by the dip in the ℓ<30\ell<30 Planck temperature data. The parameter degeneracies are illustrated in Fig. 25.

The ALA_{\rm L} results appear to be robust to changes in foreground modelling in the baseline likelihood, with the CamSpec 545 GHz cleaned likelihood (see Appendix A) giving very similar results. However, the dip in the residuals at 1420≲ℓ≲14801420\la\ell\la 1480, part of the oscillatory feature that looks like additional lensing, nearly coincides with an approximately 3​σ3\thinspace\sigma discrepancy (for the best-fit foreground cosmology model) between the 143-GHz and 217-GHz power spectra at 1450≲ℓ≲15101450\la\ell\la 1510, with the 217-GHz spectrum pulling the coadded spectrum low compared to 143 GHz by an amount comparable to the coadded residual (at ℓ=1480\ell=1480 the 217-GHz spectrum is 𝒟ℓ≈7​μ\mathcal{D}_{\ell}\approx 7\thinspace\muK2 lower than 143 GHz with smoothing σℓ=40\sigma_{\ell}=40; see 293). This may be an indication that the preference for ALA_{\rm L} at high multipoles is partly due to unknown systematics or foregrounds. However, tightly cutting the ℓ\ell range that contributes to the 3​σ3\thinspace\sigma frequency difference does not in itself shift ALA_{\rm L} to substantially lower values (though cutting all of 1420≲ℓ≲14801420\la\ell\la 1480 does), and the significance of the oscillatory feature in the Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} CMB residual is in any case not very high. If it is largely a statistical fluctuation, it would be expected to vary with changes in sky area; that is somewhat the case, with around 80%80\thinspace\% sky area giving a substantially less oscillatory residual to the same best-fit Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model at ℓ≲1600\ell\la 1600, but still favouring high ALA_{\rm L}. Different power spectrum analyses have also shown the preference for ALA_{\rm L} (Spergel et al. 2015; Couchot et al. 2017), though with varying significance, which could indicate that our roughly 3​σ3\thinspace\sigma significance is partly an issue of analysis choices, e.g., the sky areas included and foreground priors chosen.

The dashed line in Fig. 3 shows the lensing power spectrum in the Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE best-fit Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}+ALA_{\rm L} model, which is clearly inconsistent with the lensing reconstruction, since it lies above almost all of the measured data points. Because the amplitude of the lensing smoothing effect can be calculated from the lensing potential power spectrum alone, which we can also empirically measure, it is impossible to increase the lensing smoothing of the CMB peaks without also increasing the measured lensing reconstruction amplitude. This remains true if the lensing power spectrum is allowed to vary in shape (Motloch & Hu 2018). The actual lensing smoothing effect can also partly be removed by delensing, as shown by Larsen et al. (2016) and Carron et al. (2017). In 294 we update these delensing analyses, and show (using the internal lensing reconstruction, a Planck CIB map as a tracer of the lensing potential, and a combined estimate) that the amount of peak sharpening observed after delensing is consistent with theoretical expectations (e.g., for the T​TTT spectrum, we measure a reduction in lensing smoothing of 0.411±0.0280.411\pm 0.028, compared to the expected value of 0.3750.375 when using a combination of CIB and Planck lensing reconstruction).

Although the residuals shown in Fig. 24 between the data and the Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} best fit temperature spectrum show what looks like an oscillatory lensing residual at high ℓ\ell, the fit itself is determined by the entire range of multipoles (and the low-ℓ\ell polarization than constrains τ\tau). The preference for AL>1A_{\rm L}>1 could therefore be attributed to other scales when considering the CMB spectra alone. For example, after removing ℓ<30\ell<30 in both temperature and polarization, ALA_{\rm L} from T​TTT is consistent with unity to within 1​σ1\thinspace\sigma. However, in this case the Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} lensing amplitudes are still large, giving a value of Ωm​σ80.25\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}\sigma_{8}^{0.25}, in 2​σ2\thinspace\sigma tension with the lensing reconstruction. This is another reflection of the tension noted in Sect. 6.1 between the lensing reconstruction and the lensing amplitude predicted using temperature multipoles ℓ≳800\ell\ga 800: the two tensions are therefore not independent and largely driven by the same features of the Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} fit to the temperature and low-ℓ\ell polarization data.

If AL>1A_{\rm L}>1 is not just a statistical fluctuation, but comes from new physics changing the theoretical predictions, it could be something that mimics the smoothing effect in the CMB peaks. The lensing smoothing effect comes from averaging over the sky a spectrum that is locally varying (due to magnification and shear locally changing the scale and shape of the CMB peaks). Conceptually, the temperature lensing reconstruction works by looking for this spatial variation in scale and shear of the local power. Any non-lensing isotropic change in the amplitude of the small-scale peaks and troughs, either from new physics or random fluctuations, would therefore only have a small effect on the lensing reconstruction, which is sensitive to scale and shape, not amplitude.

One locally anisotropic physical effect that has been considered as a possible explanation is the presence of large-scale compensated isocurvature modes, discussed in detail in Planck Collaboration X (2020). Because the large-scale isocurvature modes locally vary the baryon-to-photon ratio, they can partially mimic the lensing smoothing effect by spatially varying the acoustic scale (Muñoz et al. 2016; Valiviita 2017). However, because they have a similar local effect to lensing, they also affect the large-scale lensing reconstruction (Smith et al. 2017). Combining with the Planck 2018 lensing reconstruction, which now extends down to L=8L=8, as shown in Planck Collaboration X (2020) this model therefore does not offer a significant improvement in overall fit (Δ​χeff2=−3.3\Delta\chi^{2}_{\rm eff}=-3.3 with Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing).

If the AL>1A_{\rm L}>1 preference is simply a statistical excursion (perhaps the most likely explanation), this indicates that there are random features in the spectrum that are pulling some parameters unusually far from expected values.3030 30 It is not trivial to assess how unlikely a fluctuation in a consistency parameter like this is given the number of different cosmological and consistency test parameters we might have looked at. We are only discussing ALA_{\rm L} in detail here because it comes out high; other consistency parameters, for example the relative amplitude of ISW, Doppler, and Sachs-Wolfe contributions to the temperature spectrum, come out perfectly consistent with expectations. There are several theoretical models that can fit the CMB power spectra and also predict larger lensing amplitudes. These include Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} models with spatial curvature, for which we find ΩK<0\Omega_{K}<0 at over 3​σ3\thinspace\sigma (Sect. 7.3) from the CMB power spectra, and some dark energy and modified gravity models (Sect. 7.4). For extensions to base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, parameters that decrease the lensing amplitude are more constrained by the Planck power spectra than might otherwise be expected; for example, higher neutrino masses lower the predicted lensing power compared to base Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, leading to surprisingly tight constraints (Sect. 7.5.1). Adding the lensing-reconstruction information significantly reduces the parameter space of larger lensing amplitudes and partially mitigates these effects. However, the statistical power of the Planck power spectra is sufficiently high that the joint constraints prefer lensing amplitudes in the higher range allowed by the lensing data.

Even within Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, the fact that the data prefer more lensing leads to a preference for higher fluctuation amplitudes, hence the high-ℓ\ell data yield higher AsA_{\rm s} and higher τ\tau than we infer in combination with large-scale EE-mode polarization (Sect. 2.2.3) or lensing reconstruction. Since these preferences are degenerate with Ωm​h2\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}h^{2}, nsn_{\rm s}, and H0H_{0} (see 276, 284), these parameters are also pulled (Ωm​h2\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}h^{2} higher, nsn_{\rm s} and H0H_{0} lower). Our baseline best-fit results include both the “lowE” data and the lensing reconstruction, each of which restrict the range of allowed variation, so the remaining pulls should be modest; however, it should not perhaps be too much of a surprise if the central values of the parameters inferred from Planck turn out to be slightly more shifted than typical with respect to the ultimate truth if the base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model is correct.

7 Extensions to the base-𝚲\boldsymbol{\Lambda}CDM model

7.1 Grid of extended models

We have studied a range of extension to the base Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model. A full grid of results from standard parameter extensions is available online through the 273.3131 31 Chains are available at https://pla.esac.esa.int, with description and parameter tables in Planck Collaboration ES (2018). Figure 26 and Table 4 summarize the constraints on 1-parameter extensions to the base-Λ\LambdaCDM model. As in 2013 and 2015 we find no strong evidence in favour of any of these extensions, using either the Planck data alone or Planck combined with BAO. We also find that constraints on the base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} parameters are remarkably robust to a variety of possible extensions to the Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model, as shown in Table 5: many of these parameters are constrained to high precision in a nearly model-independent way.

We now discuss some specific extensions in more detail.

7.2 Early Universe

CMB observations probe the state of the universe at the earliest time that is directly observable with the electromagnetic spectrum. The physics of the anisotropies is well understood, and can be predicted accurately with linear theory given a set of initial conditions. Planck observations can therefore be used to give powerful constraints on the initial conditions, i.e., the perturbations present at the start of the hot big bang. We discuss in turn constraints on the scalar and tensor perturbations, allowing for deviations from a purely power-law scalar spectrum, and discuss the interpretation within the context of the most popular inflationary models.

7.2.1 Primordial scalar power spectrum

The Planck data are consistent with purely adiabatic primordial scalar curvature perturbations, with no evidence for isocurvature modes (Planck Collaboration X 2020, see), as predicted by the simplest single-field inflation models. The primordial power spectrum is then just a function of scale. In this section, we characterize the scalar fluctuation spectrum in terms of a spectral index nsn_{\rm s} and its first two derivatives with respect to ln⁡k\ln k (the “running” and “running of the running” of the spectral index):

𝒫ℛ​(k)\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{R}}(k) =\displaystyle= As​(kk0)n⁡(k),\displaystyle A_{\rm s}\left(\frac{k}{k_{0}}\right)^{n(k)}, (36a)
n⁡(k)\displaystyle n(k) =\displaystyle= ns−1+(1/2)​(d​ns/d​ln⁡k)​ln⁡(k/k0)\displaystyle n_{\rm s}-1+(1/2)(dn_{\rm s}/d\ln k)\ln(k/k_{0}) (36b)
+(1/6)​(d2​ns/d​ln⁡k2)​(ln⁡(k/k0))2.\displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt+(1/6)(d^{2}n_{\rm s}/d\ln k^{2})(\ln(k/k_{0}))^{2}.

In the absence of any running of the spectral index, our constraint on nsn_{\rm s} for the base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model (Eq. 19) shows an 8​σ8\thinspace\sigma tilt away from scale invariance. Adding BAO tightens the constraint to nearly 9​σ9\thinspace\sigma:

ns=0.9665±0.0038(68 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO).\left.n_{\rm s}=0.9665\pm 0.0038\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO). \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (37)

The need for a red-tilted scalar spectrum is quite robust to extensions to base Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, as summarized in Table 5. In all cases, we find ns<1n_{\rm s}<1 at ≥3​σ\geq 3\thinspace\sigma.

Adding running of the spectral index, d​ns/d​ln⁡kdn_{\rm s}/d\ln k, as a single additional parameter to base Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, we find

d​ns/d​ln⁡k=−0.0045±0.0067,ns=0.9641±0.0044,ns,0.002=0.979±0.021,}68 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing,\left.\begin{aligned} dn_{\rm s}/d\ln k&=-0.0045\pm 0.0067,\\ n_{\rm s}&=0.9641\pm 0.0044,\\ n_{{\rm s},0.002}&=0.979\pm 0.021,\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{85.35826pt}{\begin{flushleft}68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing, \end{flushleft}}}} (38a)
d​ns/d​ln⁡k=−0.0041±0.0067,ns=0.9659±0.0040,ns,0.002=0.979±0.021,}68 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO,\left.\begin{aligned} dn_{\rm s}/d\ln k&=-0.0041\pm 0.0067,\\ n_{\rm s}&=0.9659\pm 0.0040,\\ n_{{\rm s},0.002}&=0.979\pm 0.021,\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{85.35826pt}{\begin{flushleft}68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO, \end{flushleft}}}} (38b)

where nsn_{\rm s} is defined by default at k=0.05​Mpc−1k=0.05\thinspace\text{Mpc}^{-1} and ns,0.002n_{{\rm s},0.002} is the corresponding tilt at k=0.002​Mpc−1k=0.002\thinspace\text{Mpc}^{-1}. The slight preference for negative running is driven by the mild tension between the CMB temperature power spectrum at high and low multipoles discussed in Sect. 6.1, with negative running allowing higher large-scale tilt, giving less power on large scales (see Fig. 27 and the extensive discussions in 276 and 284). The measurements of the tilt and running around the pivot scale of k≃0.05​Mpc−1k\simeq 0.05\thinspace\text{Mpc}^{-1} are robust to allowing even more freedom for the spectrum to vary with scale. For example, allowing for running of the running we find

d2​ns/d​ln⁡k2=0.009±0.012,d​ns/d​ln⁡k=0.0011±0.0099,ns=0.9647±0.0043,}68 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO.\left.\begin{aligned} d^{2}n_{\rm s}/d\ln k^{2}&=0.009\pm 0.012,\\ dn_{\rm s}/d\ln k&=0.0011\pm 0.0099,\\ n_{\rm s}&=0.9647\pm 0.0043,\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{85.35826pt}{\begin{flushleft}68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO. \end{flushleft}}}} (39)

Here the slight preference for negative running has almost disappeared, and there is instead a slight preference for lower large-scale power by having positive running of the running, leaving a near power-law solution on small scales. There is no evidence for any significant deviation from a power law on small scales. This is consistent with the simplest slow-roll inflation models where the running (and higher derivatives of the spectral index) are higher order in slow-roll (so that d​ns/d​ln⁡k=𝒪⁡(|ns−1|2)dn_{\rm s}/d\ln k=\mathcal{O}(|n_{\rm s}-1|^{2}), d2​ns/d​ln⁡k2=𝒪⁡(|ns−1|3)d^{2}n_{\rm s}/d\ln k^{2}=\mathcal{O}(|n_{\rm s}-1|^{3})) and all deviations from a constant spectral index can be neglected at Planck sensitivity.

An analysis of more general parameterizations of the primordial power spectrum are presented in section 6 of Planck Collaboration X (2020), including various specific physically motivated models, as well as general parametric reconstructions. Models with many more free parameters can provide better fits to the data, but none are favoured; in all cases the small-scale spectrum is found to be consistent with a power law over the range 0.008​Mpc−1≲k≲0.1​Mpc−10.008\thinspace\text{Mpc}^{-1}\la k\la 0.1\thinspace\text{Mpc}^{-1}, with low-significance hints of larger-scale features corresponding to the dip in the low-ℓ\ell temperature power spectrum. The introduction of the additional degrees of freedom in the initial power spectrum had no significant impact on the determination of the main cosmological parameters for the parameterizations considered.

7.2.2 Tensor modes

Primordial gravitational waves3232 32 The polarization anisotropies generated by gravitational waves was discussed first by Polnarev (1985)., or tensor modes, source a distinctive curl-like (“BB-mode”) pattern in the CMB polarization and add additional power to the large-scale temperature power spectrum (Kamionkowski et al. 1997; Seljak & Zaldarriaga 1997). Planck’s BB-mode measurement is noise and systematics limited and provides a relative weak constraint on the tensor-to-scalar ratio r0.002< 0.41r_{0.002}\thinspace{<}\thinspace 0.41 (95 % CL, Planck Collaboration V 2020). As with the 2013 and 2015 releases, the strongest constraint on tensor modes from the Planck data alone comes from the T​TTT spectrum at ℓ≲100\ell\la 100.

The precision of the Planck temperature constraint remains limited by cosmic variance from the scalar component and is model dependent. The tightest and least model-dependent constraints on the tensor amplitude come from the Ade et al. (2018, BK15) analysis of the BICEP2/Keck field, in combination with Planck and WMAP maps to remove polarized Galactic dust emission. The BK15 observations measure the BB-mode polarization power spectrum in nine bins at ℓ≲300\ell\la 300, with the tensor amplitude information coming mainly from scales ℓ≃100\ell\simeq 100, where the BB-mode spectrum from scattering at recombination is expected to peak. The Planck CMB power spectrum measurements use a much larger sky area, and are useful to convert this measurement into a constraint on the tensor-to-scalar ratio rr at a given scale with little additional cosmic variance error. To relate the tensor measurement to constraints on specific inflation models (which usually predict a region in the nsn_{\rm s}–rr plane), combining with the Planck data is also essential, although model dependent.

Figure 28 shows the constraints in the nsn_{\rm s}–rr plane, with rr added as a single additional parameter to the base model and plotted at pivot scale 0.002​Mpc−10.002\thinspace\text{Mpc}^{-1}. We assume the tensor-mode spectrum is close to scale invariant, with spectral index given by the inflation consistency relation to second order in slow-roll parameters. Planck alone gives

r0.002<0.10,(95%,TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing),r_{0.002}<0.10,\quad(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ \text{TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE+lensing}), (40)

with ns=0.9659±0.0041n_{\rm s}=0.9659\pm 0.0041 at 1​σ1\thinspace\sigma. Adding BK15 to directly measure the tensor amplitude significantly tightens the rr constraint, and adding BAO data tightens (slightly) the nsn_{\rm s} constraint. Using the Planck temperature likelihoods we find

r0.002<0.055(95 %, TT+lowE+lensing+BK15+BAO),\left.r_{0.002}<0.055\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{170.71652pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BK15\allowbreak+BAO), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (41)

with ns=0.9661±0.0040n_{\rm s}=0.9661\pm 0.0040 at 1​σ1\thinspace\sigma, or adding polarization

r0.002<0.058(95 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BK15+BAO),\left.r_{0.002}<0.058\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BK15\allowbreak+BAO), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (42)

with ns=0.9668±0.0037n_{\rm s}=0.9668\pm 0.0037 at 1​σ1\thinspace\sigma. However, the small change when adding polarization is not stable to the choice of polarization likelihood; when using the CamSpec TT,TE,EE+lowE likelihood in place of Plik, we find the weaker constraint r0.002<0.065r_{0.002}<0.065 for the same data combination as that used in Eq. (42).

All the combined nsn_{\rm s}–rr contours exclude convex potentials at about the 95%95\thinspace\% confidence (marginally less if we use the CamSpec likelihood, see Fig. 28), which substantially restricts the range of allowed inflation models and disfavours all simple integer power law potentials. More generally, since rr depends on the slope of the potential, the smallness of the empirical upper limit on rr implies that the inflationary potential must have been nearly flat when modes exited the horizon. The measured nsn_{\rm s} must then be determined largely by the second derivative of the potential, suggesting a hierarchy in the magnitudes of the slow-roll parameters, favouring hilltop-like potentials. For a detailed discussion of the implications for specific inflation models see Planck Collaboration X (2020).

If we allow running of the spectral index in addition to tensor modes, the constraint on r0.002r_{0.002} weakens if we use only the Planck likelihood; a negative running allows nsn_{\rm s} at large scales to shift to higher values, lowering the large-scale scalar amplitude, and hence allowing a larger tensor contribution. Inclusion of the BK15 likelihood significantly reduces the extent of this degeneracy by constraining the tensor amplitude more directly, giving

r0.002<0.16,d​ns/d​ln⁡k=−0.008−0.015+0.014,}   95 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE  +lensing,  \left.\begin{aligned} r_{0.002}&<0.16,\\ dn_{\rm s}/d\ln k&=-0.008^{+0.014}_{-0.015},\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{113.81102pt}{\begin{flushleft}95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\\ +lensing, \end{flushleft}}}} (43a)
r0.002<0.066,d​ns/d​ln⁡k=−0.006±0.013,}   95 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE  +lensing+BK15+BAO.  \left.\begin{aligned} r_{0.002}&<0.066,\\ dn_{\rm s}/d\ln k&=-0.006\pm 0.013,\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{99.58464pt}{\begin{flushleft}95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\\ +lensing+BK15+BAO. \end{flushleft}}}} (43b)

The combination of Planck and BK15 robustly constrain the tensor ratio to be small, with r0.002≲0.06r_{0.002}\la 0.06. The implications for inflation are slightly more model dependent as a result of degeneracies between nsn_{\rm s} and additional parameters in extended Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} models. However, as shown in Table 5, the extensions of Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} that we consider in this paper cannot substantially shift the value of the spectral index when the tensor amplitude is small, so the overall conclusions are unlikely to change substantially in extended models.

7.3 Spatial curvature

The base-Λ\LambdaCDM model assumes that the spatial hypersurfaces are flat, such as would be predicted (to within measurable precision) by the simplest inflationary models. This is a prediction that can be tested to high accuracy by the combination of CMB and BAO data (the CMB alone suffers from a geometric degeneracy, which is weakly broken with the addition of CMB lensing). This is illustrated in Fig. 29.

The combination of the Planck temperature and polarization power spectra give

ΩK=−0.056−0.018+0.028(68 %, Planck TT+lowE),\left.\Omega_{K}=-0.056^{+0.028}_{-0.018}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT\allowbreak+lowE), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (44a)
ΩK=−0.044−0.015+0.018(68 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE),\left.\Omega_{K}=-0.044^{+0.018}_{-0.015}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (44b)

an apparent detection of curvature at well over 2​σ2\thinspace\sigma. The 99%99\thinspace\% probability region for the TT,TE,EE+lowE result is −0.095<ΩK<−0.007-0.095<\Omega_{K}<-0.007, with only about 1/10000 samples at ΩK≥0\Omega_{K}\geq 0. This is not entirely a volume effect, since the best-fit χ2\chi^{2} changes by Δ​χeff2=−11\Delta\chi^{2}_{\rm eff}=-11 compared to base Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} when adding the one additional curvature parameter. The reasons for the pull towards negative values of ΩK\Omega_{K} are discussed at length in 284 and Sect. 6.2. They are essentially the same as those that lead to the preference for AL>1A_{\rm L}>1, although slightly exacerbated in the case of curvature, since the low multipoles also fit the low-ℓ\ell temperature likelihood slightly better if ΩK<0\Omega_{K}<0. As with the AL>1A_{\rm L}>1 preference, the joint Planck polarization result is not robust at the approximately 0.5​σ0.5\thinspace\sigma level to modelling of the polarization likelihoods, with the CamSpec TT,TE,EE+lowE likelihood giving ΩK=−0.037−0.014+0.019\Omega_{K}=-0.037^{+0.019}_{-0.014}.

Closed models predict substantially higher lensing amplitudes than in Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, so combining with the lensing reconstruction (which is consistent with a flat model) pulls parameters back into consistency with a spatially flat universe to well within 2​σ2\thinspace\sigma:

ΩK=−0.0106±0.0065(68 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing).\left.\Omega_{K}=-0.0106\pm 0.0065\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{113.81102pt}{\begin{flushleft}(68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing). \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (45a)

The constraint can be further sharpened by combining the Planck data with BAO data; this convincingly breaks the geometric degeneracy to give

ΩK=0.0007±0.0019(68 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO).\left.\Omega_{K}=0.0007\pm 0.0019\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{113.81102pt}{\begin{flushleft}(68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO). \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (45b)

The joint results suggests our Universe is spatially flat to a 1​σ1\thinspace\sigma accuracy of 0.2%0.2\thinspace\%.

7.4 Dark energy and modified gravity

The late-time accelerated expansion of the Universe (Riess et al. 1998; Perlmutter et al. 1999) is still considered one of the most mysterious aspects of the standard cosmology. In the base Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model the acceleration is driven by a cosmological constant, added into the Einstein equations of General Relativity (Einstein 1917, GR,). Although Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} fits the data well, Λ\Lambda is a phenomenological parameter without an underlying theoretical basis to explain its value (Weinberg 1987, though see). In addition, the empirically required value of Λ\Lambda marks our epoch as a special time in the evolution of the Universe. Attempts have therefore been made to find a dynamical mechanism that leads to cosmic acceleration, with evolving background energy densities close to Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}. Such dynamics is usually associated with a fluid (a scalar field) which we refer to as “dark energy” (DE), or with modifications of GR, which we refer to as “modified gravity” (MG).

A detailed analysis of the impact of Planck data on dark energy and modified gravity was presented in a dedicated paper that accompanied the 2015 Planck release, (Planck Collaboration XIV 2016, hereafter 285). We refer the reader to this paper for a review of different cosmological models, and for constraints from Planck on its own and in combination with galaxy weak lensing (WL) and redshift-space distortions (RSDs). In 285 it was shown that although the base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model fits Planck data, there were some tensions (at levels as high as 3​σ3\thinspace\sigma) when Planck was combined with RSD and WL data, even when conservative cuts were applied to exclude nonlinear scales. However, the addition of Planck lensing data was found to reduce these tensions. Updated constraints on a few specific models, using more recent WL data, are presented in DES Collaboration (2018b).

In this paper, we follow a similar methodology to 285, distinguishing between models that directly affect only the background (and impact perturbations predominantly through changes in the expansion rate) and those that directly affect perturbations. However, we restrict the analysis to a smaller range of models here. As in the rest of this paper, we show results for the baseline Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing data set and for combinations with other relevant data sets. Such external data are particularly useful for constraining DE and MG models because the largest deviations from Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} are usually at late times, which are not well constrained by the CMB power-spectra and CMB lensing. However, CMB lensing provides important information that mitigates the preference for AL> 1A_{\rm L}\thinspace{>}\thinspace 1 seen in the Planck temperature power spectra (Sect. 6.2), so we explicitly comment on the impact of CMB lensing wherever relevant. We recall here that the lensing likelihood assumes a fiducial Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model, but linear corrections to the fiducial mode are accounted for self-consistently. 294 explicitly tested that this procedure is unbiased, even when the lensing spectrum differs from the fiducial spectrum by as much as 20 % (which is much larger than differences allowed by the CMB lensing data).

We consider the following external data sets:

  • •

    SNe + BAO (see Sects. 5.1, 5.2, and 5.4 for discussions of the data sets and comments on why we do not combine Planck data with direct measurements of H0H_{0});

  • •

    RSDs (as described in Sect. 5.3), where we specifically use BOSS-DR12 data from Alam et al. (2017), adopting the f​σ8f\sigma_{8}–HH–DMD_{\rm M} parameterization;

  • •

    WL data from DES (as described in Sect. 5.5), except that here we use the Weyl potential to obtain theoretical predictions for the lensing correlation functions, rather than assuming the matter-sourced Poisson equation to relate the lensing potential power spectrum to the matter power spectrum.

We calculate all results both fixing and varying the neutrino mass. Neutrino masses are known to be degenerate with DE and MG and should be varied consistently when testing such models (Dirian 2017, as discussed in); fixing the neutrino mass to the minimal value of 0.06​eV0.06\thinspace{\rm eV} (as for our baseline Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} results) gives tighter constraints than allowing the neutrino mass to vary and partly shifts results towards Λ\LambdaCDM. These shifts are usually small, often negligible, and always less than 1​σ1\thinspace\sigma for marginalized results. We model the small-scale nonlinear power spectrum using HMcode (Mead et al. 2015; Mead et al. 2016) as in the main parameter grid of extensions to base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, neglecting any differences arising from modified gravity. In using the DES weak-lensing correlation functions, we exclude scales where nonlinear modelling uncertainties are important, but since the modified gravity models introduce an additional level of uncertainty, we also marginalize over the feedback amplitude BB with a flat prior, 2≤B≤42\leq B\leq 4. This parameter is used by HMcode to introduce an additional uncertainty in the nonlinear correction due to the modelling of the baryonic effects on the matter power spectrum at small scales, modifying the halo mass-concentration relation and the shape of the halo density profile. In this context, however, we marginalize over this parameter in order to reduce the residual sensitivity of our results on the nonlinear modelling in modified gravity theories; marginalizing over BB reduces the constraining power coming from nonlinear scales, where the correction recipe used by HMcode may not correctly reproduce the perturbation evolution for all the models included in our parameterization.

Throughout this section we will adopt the metric given by the line element

d​s2=a2​[−(1+2​Ψ)​d​τ2+(1−2​Φ)​d​x2],ds^{2}=a^{2}\left[-(1+2\Psi)d\tau^{2}+(1-2\Phi)dx^{2}\right]\thinspace, (46)

with the speed of light cc set to 1. The functions Φ⁡(τ,x)\Phi(\tau,x) and Ψ⁡(τ,x)\Psi(\tau,x) are the gauge-invariant gravitational potentials, which are very nearly equal at late times in Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}. For the background parameterization we use the standard CAMB code, while for the perturbation parameterization we use the publicly available code MGCAMB3333 33 Available at http://www.sfu.ca/~aha25/MGCAMB.html (February 2014 version, but updated to correctly output the power spectrum of the Weyl potential). (Zhao et al. 2009; Hojjati et al. 2011) integrated into the latest version of CosmoMC. For the effective field theory (EFT) models of Sect. 7.4.3 we use EFTCAMB3434 34 Available at http://eftcamb.org/ (version 2.0). (Hu et al. 2014; Raveri et al. 2014).

7.4.1 Background parameterization: w0w_{0}, waw_{a}

If the DE is a generic dynamical fluid, its equation of state parameter w≡p/ρw\equiv p/\rho will in general be a function of time. Here pp and ρ\rho are the spatially-averaged (background) DE pressure and density.

To test a time-varying equation of state we adopt the functional form

w⁡(a)=w0+(1−a)​wa,w(a)=w_{0}+(1-a)w_{a}\thinspace, (47)

where w0w_{0} and waw_{a} are assumed to be constants. In Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, w0=−1w_{0}=-1 and wa=0w_{a}=0. We use the parameterized post-Friedmann (PPF) model of Fang et al. (2008) to explore expansion histories where ww crosses −1-1. The PPF equations are modelled on the perturbations of quintessence dark energy, i.e., they correspond to a fluid with vanishing anisotropic stress and a rest-frame speed of sound approximately equal to the speed of light. Because of the high sound speed, dark-energy density perturbations are suppressed inside the horizon and are irrelevant compared to the matter perturbations, except on the very largest scales. While this is the standard procedure adopted in the literature, we should emphasize that a single minimally-coupled canonical scalar field (quintessence) cannot cross w=−1w=-1 (Vikman 2005). Such a crossing could happen in models with two scalar fields (one of which would have to be a phantom field with the opposite sign of the kinetic term); in such models the perturbations remain close to the quintessence case (Kunz & Sapone 2006, see e.g.,). Alternatively, the phantom “barrier” can be crossed with a sound speed that vanishes in the phantom domain (Creminelli et al. 2009) or in models with additional terms in the action, such as in kinetic-gravity-braiding (Deffayet et al. 2010), or with non-minimal couplings (Amendola 2000; Pettorino & Baccigalupi 2008). These and other modified gravity models, typically also change the behaviour of the perturbations.

Marginalized contours of the posterior distributions for w0w_{0} and waw_{a} are shown in Fig. 30. Note that CMB lensing has only a small effect on the constraints from Planck alone (see the parameter grid tables in the 273). Using Planck data alone, a wide volume of dynamical dark-energy parameter space is allowed, with contours cut off by our priors (−3<w0<1-3<w_{0}<1, −5<wa<5-5<w_{a}<5, and 0.4<h<10.4<h<1; note that Fig. 30 does not show the complete prior range). However, most of the allowed region of parameter space corresponds to phantom models with very high values of H0H_{0} (as discussed in 285); such models are inconsistent with the late-time evolution constrained by SNe and BAO data. This is illustrated in Fig. 30 which also shows constraints if we add BAO/RSD+WL and BAO+SNe to the Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing likelihood. The addition of external data sets narrows the constraints towards the Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} values of w0=−1w_{0}=-1, wa=0w_{a}=0. The tightest constraints are found for the data combination Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO+SNe; the difference in χ2\chi^{2} between the best-fit DE and Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} models for this data combination is only Δ​χ2=−1.4\Delta\chi^{2}=-1.4 (which is not significant given the two additional parameters). Numerical constraints for these data combinations, as well as χ2\chi^{2} differences, are presented in Table 6. It is also apparent that for the simple w0w_{0}, waw_{a} parameterization of evolving DE, Planck combined with external data sets does not allow significantly lower values of S8S_{8} or higher values of H0H_{0} compared to the base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} cosmology.

Fixing the evolution parameter wa=0w_{a}=0, we obtain the tight constraint

w0=−1.028±0.031(68 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+SNe+BAO),\left.w_{0}=-1.028\pm 0.031\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+{SNe}\allowbreak+BAO), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (48)

and restricting to w0>−1w_{0}>-1 (i.e., not allowing phantom equations of state), we find

w0<−0.95(95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+SNe+BAO).\left.w_{0}<-0.95\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{156.49014pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+{SNe}\allowbreak+BAO). \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (49)

Here we only quote two significant figures, so that the result is robust to differences between the Plik and CamSpec likelihoods.

For the remainder of this section, we assume Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} at the background level (i.e., w=−1w=-1 at all times), but instead turn our attention to constraining the behaviour of the dark sector perturbations.

7.4.2 Perturbation parameterization: μ\mu, η\eta

In the types of DE or MG models considered here, changes to observables only arise via the impact on the geometry of the Universe. At the level of perturbations, it is then sufficient to model the impact on the gravitational potentials Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi, or, equivalently, on two independent combinations of these potentials (Zhang et al. 2007; Amendola et al. 2008, e.g.,). Following 285 we consider two phenomenological functions, μ\mu and η\eta, defined as follows.

  1. 1.

    μ⁡(a,k)\mu(a,k): a modification of the Poisson equation for Ψ\Psi,

    k2​Ψ=−μ⁡(a,k)​ 4​π​G​a2​[ρ​Δ+3​(ρ+P)​σ],k^{2}\Psi=-\mu(a,k)\thinspace 4\pi Ga^{2}\left[\rho\Delta+3(\rho+P)\sigma\right], (50)

    where ρ​Δ=ρm​Δm+ρr​Δr\rho\Delta=\rho_{\rm m}\Delta_{\rm m}+\rho_{\rm r}\Delta_{\rm r}, using comoving fractional density perturbations Δ\Delta, and where σ\sigma is the anisotropic stress from relativistic species (photons and neutrinos).

  2. 2.

    η⁡(a,k)\eta(a,k): an effective additional anisotropic stress, leading to a difference between the gravitational potentials Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi, defined implicitly through

    k2​[Φ−η⁡(a,k)​Ψ]=μ⁡(a,k)​ 12​π​G​a2​(ρ+P)​σ.k^{2}\left[\Phi-\eta(a,k)\Psi\right]=\mu(a,k)\thinspace 12\pi Ga^{2}(\rho+P)\sigma. (51)

    At late times, σ\sigma from standard particles is negligible and we find

    η⁡(a,k)≈Φ/Ψ.\eta(a,k)\approx\Phi/\Psi. (52)

These definitions are phenomenological, in the sense that they are not derived from a theoretical action. However, they are able to capture a generic deviation of the perturbation evolution from Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} that does not need to correspond to a known model. This approach is complementary to constraints on action-based models, which are the topic of the next subsection. When η=μ=1\eta=\mu=1 we recover GR at all times, including when there are non-zero contribution from photons and neutrinos to the density perturbation or anisotropic stress. In the parameterization adopted here (described further below), the MG contribution to η\eta is only relevant at late times, when the anisotropic stress from relativistic particles is negligible.

In this section we fix the background evolution to that of Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} (w=−1w=-1 at all times), so that any significant deviation of μ\mu or η\eta from unity would indicate a deviation from Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}. We also consider constraints on the derived quantity Σ\Sigma, defined as

k2​[Φ+Ψ]=−Σ⁡(a,k)​4​π​G​a2​[2​ρ​Δ−3​(ρ+P)​σ].k^{2}\left[\Phi+\Psi\right]=-\Sigma(a,k)4\pi Ga^{2}\left[2\rho\Delta-3(\rho+P)\sigma\right]. (53)

Since Σ\Sigma measures deviations of the lensing potential from the GR prediction, it is better constrained by WL data than μ\mu and η\eta separately.

For simplicity we only allow μ\mu and η\eta to vary with time (as in 285). Scale dependence increases the number of degeneracies in parameter space and may require, for example, higher-order statistics in WL observables (Peel et al. 2018) to break the degeneracies. We use the late-time DE parameterization of 285 and Casas et al. (2017), where the time evolution of all quantities is assumed to be proportional to the relative dark-energy density:

μ⁡(z)=1+E11​ΩDE​(z);\mu(z)=1+E_{11}\Omega_{\rm DE}(z); (54a)
η⁡(z)=1+E21​ΩDE​(z).\eta(z)=1+E_{21}\Omega_{\rm DE}(z). (54b)

This defines the constants E11E_{11} and E21E_{21}. We report results in terms of μ0≡μ⁡(z=0)\mu_{0}\equiv\mu(z=0) and η0≡η⁡(z=0)\eta_{0}\equiv\eta(z=0), which are determined from E11E_{11} and E21E_{21}, given the dark-energy density parameter today. This parameterization is motivated by the assumption that the impact of dark energy depends on its density and therefore allows for more deviation of μ\mu and η\eta from Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} at late times. The alternative early-time parameterization included in 285 led to similar results and is not discussed here for brevity. Our choice of parameterization, of course, limits the nature of possible deviations from Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}; however, the choices of Eqs. (54a) and (54b) allow us to compare our results directly with those of 285.

Figure 31 shows the marginalized constraints on μ0\mu_{0} and η0\eta_{0} from different combinations of data, and also compares with the results from 285. Marginalized mean values and errors for cosmological parameters are presented in Table 7. This table also lists results for ⟨d2⟩1/2\langle d^{2}\rangle^{1/2}, the root-mean-square CMB lensing deflection angle, and the parameter combination Σ0​S8\Sigma_{0}S_{8} that is well-constrained by the DES WL data. These quantities allow the reader to assess the impact of lensing data on the parameter constraints. The μ\mu parameter affects the growth of structure, so, for example, higher μ\mu gives larger values of σ8\sigma_{8}. The CMB only constrains MG via the integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect (on large scales, where there is large cosmic variance) and CMB lensing. Lensing observations do not constrain the fluctuation amplitude directly, but the amplitude scaled by Σ\Sigma (as defined in Eq. 53). The degeneracy direction shown in Fig. 31 corresponds to approximately constant lensing amplitude, with higher μ0\mu_{0} requiring lower Σ0\Sigma_{0} and hence lower η0\eta_{0}. The thickness of the degeneracy contour and its location depends on the constraint on lensing. With Planck data alone, or Planck+SNe+BAO, the lensing amplitude is pulled to high values by the preference for more lensing discussed in Sect. 6.2, so the contours are slightly shifted with respect to Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}. The inclusion of WL3535 35 Tests during the writing of this paper revealed a bug in MGCAMB that was also present in 2015. This bug reduced the constraining power of WL data for the (μ,η\mu,\eta) parameterization (which in 2015 was suppressed by the very conservative excision of nonlinear scales). The CMB and BAO/RSD constraints and other cosmological models were not affected by this bug. data shrinks the contour, and reduces the offset with respect to Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}; DES WL data disfavour higher lensing amplitudes than predicted by the Planck Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} cosmology. DES also measures lensing at much lower redshift than CMB lensing, so it is a more powerful probe of MG models where changes to GR only appear at late times (as we have assumed).

The BAO/RSD data constrain μ0\mu_{0} directly, since redshift distortions are a probe of structure growth. The lower panel of Fig. 31 shows constraints with BAO/RSD alone, and also demonstrates that removing the CMB lensing reconstruction data shifts the contour further from Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}; this is consistent with the pull away from Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} being driven by the preference for more lensing in the high-ℓ\ell CMB power spectra.

We can further demonstrate the effect of CMB lensing by varying the consistency parameter ALA_{\rm L} within MG models. Figure 32 shows the degeneracy between ALA_{\rm L} and Σ0−1\Sigma_{0}-1, which is computed as a derived parameter in our (μ,η\mu,\eta) parameterization. Here ALA_{\rm L} affects lensing of the CMB power spectra only, while Σ0\Sigma_{0} encodes modifications to the lensing amplitude caused by modifications of gravity. The contours show that MG models (Σ0≠1\Sigma_{0}\neq 1) are preferred by the Planck power spectra (although not strongly) if AL=1A_{\rm L}=1. The preference for higher Σ0\Sigma_{0} values is reduced by allowing larger ALA_{\rm L}; the preference for MG that we find is therefore largely another reflection of the preference for AL>1A_{\rm L}>1 discussed in Sect. 6.2. Adding Planck CMB lensing measurements shifts the contours back into consistency with Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} (blue contours). Adding BAO/RSD + WL tightens the constrains (red contours) which remain consistent with Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}. Using the CamSpec likelihood gives slightly less preference for high ALA_{\rm L}, and the results for Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing shift by about 0.2​σ0.2\thinspace\sigma towards better consistency with Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}.

7.4.3 Effective field theory description of dark energy

To investigate action-based models that can give interesting values of μ\mu and η\eta, we limit ourselves to a sub-class of effective field theories (Cheung et al. 2008; Creminelli et al. 2009; Gubitosi et al. 2013, EFTs,). The EFTs we consider contain models with a single scalar field and at most second-order equations of motion, a restriction that is in general necessary to avoid the so-called Ostrogradski instability. In addition, EFTs typically assume a universal coupling to gravity; models with non-universal couplings (Amendola 2000; Pettorino & Baccigalupi 2008), multiple scalar fields, additional vector (Hellings & Nordtvedt 1973) or tensor fields (Hassan et al. 2012), or non-local models (Belgacem et al. 2018) do not fall into this class and are not considered here. Nevertheless EFTs provide a general set of models for which we can, in principle, compute all quantities of interest, including μ\mu and η\eta (which will span a restricted part of the μ\mu–η\eta space considered in the previous section.)

As described in section 5.2.1 of 285, the degrees of freedom in actions of this class of models can be reduced to the expansion rate HH and five additional functions of time (Gleyzes et al. 2013; Bellini & Sawicki 2014) {αM,αK,αB,αT,αH\alpha_{\rm M},\alpha_{\rm K},\alpha_{\rm B},\alpha_{\rm T},\alpha_{\rm H}}. However, measurements of the speed of gravitational waves (Abbott et al. 2017) imply that αT​(z= 0)≃0\alpha_{T}(z\thinspace{=}\thinspace 0)\simeq 0, which reduces the space of acceptable models (Lombriser & Taylor 2016; McManus et al. 2016; Creminelli & Vernizzi 2017; Ezquiaga & Zumalacarregui 2017; Sakstein & Jain 2017; Baker et al. 2017).

Apart from models where gravitational wave propagation is not modified at all, which would necessarily limit us to η=1\eta=1 (Saltas et al. 2014), only conformally (non-minimally) coupled models3636 36 Recently the EFT action has been extended to include degenerate higher-order theories (Zumalacárregui & García-Bellido 2014; Gleyzes et al. 2015; Ben Achour et al. 2016, DHOST, ), which feature an additional parameter called β1\beta_{\rm 1} (Langlois et al. 2017). DHOST models can also give αT≈0\alpha_{\rm T}\approx 0, but αH\alpha_{\rm H} and β1\beta_{\rm 1} are constrained to be small from astrophysical tests of gravity (Crisostomi & Koyama 2018; Langlois et al. 2018; Dima & Vernizzi 2018; Saltas et al. 2018). with αB=−αM\alpha_{\rm B}=-\alpha_{\rm M} (and αH=0\alpha_{\rm H}=0) naturally lead to αT=0\alpha_{\rm T}=0. For these reasons we focus on this latter class of models (and for simplicity we assume αT​(z)≃0\alpha_{\rm T}(z)\simeq 0 at all times), and in addition choose the kinetic terms of the scalar (set by αK\alpha_{\rm K}) to keep the scalar sound speed equal to the speed of light (current observational data are not able to constrain the sound speed significantly, see e.g., the kk-essence model constraints in 285). We finally end up with a non-minimally coupled kk-essence model described by the single function αM\alpha_{\rm M} that determines the running of the Planck mass. The background expansion is chosen to be the same as in Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, as in our analysis of the μ\mu–η\eta parameterization described in the previous section. The main difference relative to 285 is that we now allow for αM<0\alpha_{\rm M}<0, which corresponds to a Planck mass decreasing with time.

As in 285 we adopt the parameterization αM=αM​0​aβ\alpha_{M}=\alpha_{M0}a^{\thinspace\beta}, where αM​0\alpha_{M0} is the value of αM\alpha_{M} today and where β>0\beta>0 determines how quickly the absolute value of αM\alpha_{M} decreases at high redshift. In terms of the non-minimal coupling function Ω\Omega multiplying the Ricci scalar RR in the action, this corresponds to3737 37 This notation is conventional; note that ΩEFT\Omega^{\mathrm{EFT}} here is not the contribution to the critical density, and Ω0EFT\Omega_{0}^{\mathrm{EFT}} is not the value of ΩEFT​(a)\Omega^{\mathrm{EFT}}(a) at a=1a=1.

ΩEFT​(a)=exp⁡{αM​0β​aβ}−1=exp⁡{Ω0EFT​aβ}−1,\Omega^{\mathrm{EFT}}(a)=\exp\left\{\frac{\alpha_{M0}}{\beta}a^{\thinspace\beta}\right\}-1=\exp\left\{\Omega_{0}^{\mathrm{EFT}}a^{\thinspace\beta}\right\}-1\thinspace, (55)

which agrees with the exponential model built-in to EFTCAMB (Raveri et al. 2014) (which we use to compute the model predictions presented here). The resulting posterior distribution on Ω0EFT\Omega_{0}^{\mathrm{EFT}}, marginalized over β\beta and other parameters, is shown in Fig. 33. The Λ\LambdaCDM limit lies at Ω0EFT=0\Omega_{0}^{\mathrm{EFT}}=0 (vertical dashed line). We see that the posterior distribution prefers negative values of Ω0EFT\Omega_{0}^{\mathrm{EFT}}, with a shift of 1.6​σ1.6\thinspace\sigma for the baseline Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing likelihood and 2.1​σ2.1\thinspace\sigma if CMB lensing is excluded. These shifts are reduced to 0.8​σ0.8\thinspace\sigma with the addition of BAO/RSD+WL to the Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing likelihood and to 0.9​σ0.9\thinspace\sigma if Planck lensing is excluded. Table 8 gives the parameter constraints for these data combinations and lists the changes in χ2\chi^{2} of the best fits relative to base Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}. As was the case for the (μ,η\mu,\eta) parameterization, DES WL measurements pull the contours towards Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}. If we determine μ0\mu_{0} and η0\eta_{0} that correspond to the mean values of the EFT parameters for a specific scale choice, we find that the parameters lie in the top-left quadrant of the (μ,η\mu,\eta) parameter space shown in Fig. 31. Another class of models that predicts values of (μ,η\mu,\eta) in the top-left quadrant of Fig. 31 are the non-local models, specifically the RR model of Dirian et al.
