(2016); these models are not discussed here.

Overall, the EFT sub-class of non-minimally coupled kk-essence models considered here is not preferred by current data. Without using CMB and galaxy WL lensing, Planck gives a moderate preference for models that predict more lensing compared to Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} (as found in our investigation of the (μ,η\mu,\eta) parameterization). However, combining Planck with CMB and DES WL lensing measurements disfavours high lensing amplitudes and pulls the parameters towards Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}.

7.4.4 General remarks

Planck alone provides relatively weak constraints on dark energy and modified gravity, but Planck does constrain other cosmological parameters extremely well. By combining Planck with external data we then obtain tight constraints on these models. We find no strong evidence for deviations from Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, either at the background level or when allowing for changes to the perturbations. At the background level, Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} is close to the best fit. In the simple μ\mu–η\eta and EFT parameterizations of perturbation-level deviations from GR, we do find better fits to the Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE data compared to Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, but this is largely associated with the preference in the CMB power spectra for higher lensing amplitudes (as discussed in Sect. 6.2), rather than a distinctive preference for modified gravity. Adding weak lensing data disfavours the large lensing amplitudes and our results are consistent with Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} to within 1​σ1\thinspace\sigma. Since neutrino masses are in general degenerate with DE and MG parameters, it is also worth testing the impact of varying neutrino masses versus fixing them to our base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} value of mν=0.06m_{\nu}=0.06 eV. We find similar trends, with slightly larger posteriors when varying the neutrino mass.

7.5 Neutrinos and extra relativistic species

7.5.1 Neutrino masses

The Planck base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model assumes a normal mass hierarchy with the minimal mass ∑mν=0.06\sum m_{\nu}=0.06\thinspaceeV allowed by neutrino flavour oscillation experiments. However, current observations are consistent with many neutrino mass models, and there are no compelling theoretical reasons to strongly prefer any one of them. Since the masses are already known to be non-zero, allowing for larger ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} is one of the most well-motivated extensions of the base model. The normal hierarchy, in which the lowest two mass eigenstates have the smallest mass splitting, can give any ∑mν≳0.06​eV\sum m_{\nu}\ga 0.06\thinspace\text{eV}; an inverted hierarchy, in which the two most massive eigenstates have the smallest mass separation, requires ∑mν≳0.1​eV\sum m_{\nu}\ga 0.1\thinspace\text{eV}. A constraint that ∑mν<0.1​eV\sum m_{\nu}<0.1\thinspace\text{eV} would therefore rule out the inverted hierarchy. For a review of neutrino physics and the impact on cosmology see e.g., Lesgourgues et al. (2013).

As in 276 and 284, we quote constraints assuming three species of neutrino with degenerate mass, a Fermi-Dirac distribution, and zero chemical potential. At Planck sensitivity the small mass splittings can be neglected to good accuracy (Lesgourgues & Pastor 2006, see e.g.,). Neutrinos that become non-relativistic around recombination produce distinctive signals in the CMB power spectra, which Planck and other experiments have already ruled out. If the neutrino mass is low enough that they became non-relativistic after recombination (mν≪1​eVm_{\nu}\ll 1\thinspace\text{eV}), the main effect on the CMB power spectra is a change in the angular diameter distance that is degenerate with decreasing H0H_{0}. The Planck data then mainly constrain lower masses via the lensing power spectrum and the impact of lensing on the CMB power spectra. Since the CMB power spectra prefer slightly more lensing than in the base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model, and neutrino mass can only suppress the power, we obtain somewhat stronger constraints than might be expected in typical realizations of a minimal-mass neutrino model.

In 284 no preference for higher neutrino masses was found, but a tail to high neutrino masses was still allowed, with relatively high primordial amplitudes AsA_{\rm s} combining with high neutrino mass to give acceptable lensing power. The tighter 2018 constraint on the optical depth from polarization at low multipoles restricts the primordial AsA_{\rm s} to be smaller, to match the same observed high-ℓ\ell power (Cℓ∝As​e−2​τC_{\ell}\propto A_{\rm s}e^{-2\tau}); this reduces the parameter space with larger neutrino masses, giving tighter constraints on the mass. With only temperature information at high ℓ\ell, the 95 % CL upper bound moved from 0.72 eV (284 TT+lowP) to 0.59 eV (using the SimLow polarization likelihood of Planck Collaboration Int. XLVI 2016, at low ℓ\ell). This now further tightens to

∑mν<0.54​eV(95 %, Planck TT+lowE).\left.\sum m_{\nu}<0.54\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT\allowbreak+lowE). \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (56a)

Adding high-ℓ\ell polarization further restricts residual parameter degeneracies, and the limit improves to

∑mν<0.26​eV(95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE).\left.\sum m_{\nu}<0.26\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE). \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (56b)

Although the high-ℓ\ell TT spectrum prefers more lensing than in base Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}, the lensing reconstruction is very consistent with expected amplitudes. In 284, the 2015 lensing likelihood weakened joint neutrino mass constraints because it preferred substantially less lensing than the temperature power spectrum. The 2018 lensing construction gives a slightly (1–2 %) higher lensing power spectrum amplitude than in 2015, which, combined with the decrease in the range of higher lensing amplitudes allowed by the new TT+lowE likelihood, means that the constraints are more consistent. Adding lensing therefore now slightly tightens the constraints to

∑mν\displaystyle\sum m_{\nu} <\displaystyle< 0.44​eV(95%,TT+lowE+lensing),\displaystyle 0.44\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV}\quad(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ \text{TT\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing}), (57a)
∑mν\displaystyle\sum m_{\nu} <\displaystyle< 0.24​eV(95%,TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing).\displaystyle 0.24\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV}\quad(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ \text{TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing}). (57b)

The joint constraints using polarization are however sensitive to the details of the high-ℓ\ell polarization likelihoods, with the CamSpec likelihood giving significantly weaker constraints with polarization:

∑mν\displaystyle\sum m_{\nu} <0.38​eV\displaystyle<0.38\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV}\quad (95 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE [CamSpec]) (58a)
∑mν\displaystyle\sum m_{\nu} <0.27​eV\displaystyle<0.27\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV}\quad (95 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing [CamSpec]). (58b)

As discussed in Sect. 6.2, the CamSpec TT,TE,EE+lowE likelihood shows a weaker preference for higher lensing amplitude ALA_{\rm L} than the default Plik likelihood, and this propagates directly into a weaker constraint on the neutrino mass, since for small masses the constraint is largely determined by the lensing effect. The differences between Plik and CamSpec are much smaller if we add CMB lensing, since the lensing measurements restrict the lensing amplitude to values closer to those expected in base Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}.

The combination of the acoustic scale measured by the CMB (θMC\theta_{\rm MC}) and BAO data is sufficient to largely determine the background geometry in the Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM}+∑mν\sum m_{\nu} model, since the lower-redshift BAO data break the geometric degeneracy. Combining BAO data with the CMB lensing reconstruction power spectrum (with priors on Ωb​h2\Omega_{\mathrm{b}}h^{2} and nsn_{\rm s}, following 286), the neutrino mass can also be constrained to be

∑mν<0.60​eV(95 %, Planck lensing+BAO+θMC).\left.\sum m_{\nu}<0.60\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ lensing\allowbreak+BAO\allowbreak+$\theta_{\rm MC}$). \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (59)

This number is consistent with the tighter constraints using the CMB power spectra, and almost independent of lensing effects in the CMB spectra; it would hold even if the ALA_{\rm L} tension discussed in Sect. 6.2 were interpreted as a sign of unknown residual systematics. Since the constraint from the CMB power spectra is strongly limited by the geometrical degeneracy, adding BAO data to the Planck likelihood significantly tightens the neutrino mass constraints. Without CMB lensing we find

∑mν<0.16​eV(95 %, Planck TT+lowE+BAO),\left.\sum m_{\nu}<0.16\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+BAO), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (60a)
∑mν<0.13​eV(95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+BAO),\left.\sum m_{\nu}<0.13\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+BAO), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (60b)

and combining with lensing the limits further tighten to

∑mν<0.13​eV(95 %, Planck TT+lowE+lensing+BAO),\left.\sum m_{\nu}<0.13\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (61a)
∑mν<0.12​eV(95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO).\left.\sum m_{\nu}<0.12\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO). \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (61b)

These combined constraints are almost immune to high-ℓ\ell polarization modelling uncertainties, with the CamSpec likelihood giving the 95%95\thinspace\% limit ∑mν<0.13​eV\sum m_{\nu}<0.13\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV} for Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO.

Adding the Pantheon SNe data marginally tightens the bound to ∑mν< 0.11​eV\sum m_{\nu}\thinspace{<}\thinspace 0.11\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV} (95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO+Pantheon). In contrast the full DES 1-year data prefer a slightly lower σ8\sigma_{8} value than the Planck Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} best fit, so DES slightly favours higher neutrino masses, relaxing the bound to ∑mν< 0.14​eV\sum m_{\nu}\thinspace{<}\thinspace 0.14\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV} (95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO+DES).

Increasing the neutrino mass leads to lower values of H0H_{0}, and hence aggravates the tension with the distance-ladder determination of Riess et al. (2018a, see Fig. 34). Adding the Riess et al. (2018a) H0H_{0} measurement to Planck will therefore give even tighter neutrino mass constraints (see the parameter tables in the 273), but such constraints should be interpreted cautiously until the Hubble tension is better understood.

The remarkably tight constraints using CMB and BAO data are comparable with the latest bounds from combining with Ly α\alpha forest data (Palanque-Delabrouille et al. 2015; Yèche et al. 2017). Although Ly α\alpha is a more direct probe of the neutrino mass (in the sense that it is sensitive to the matter power spectrum on scales where the suppression caused by neutrinos is expected to be significant) the measurements are substantially more difficult to model and interpret than the CMB and BAO data. Our 95%95\thinspace\% limit of ∑mν<0.12​eV\sum m_{\nu}<0.12\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV} starts to put pressure on the inverted mass hierarchy (which requires ∑mν≳0.1​eV\sum m_{\nu}\ga 0.1\thinspace\text{eV}) independently of Ly α\alpha data. This is consistent with constraints from neutrino laboratory experiments which also slightly prefer the normal hierarchy at 22–3​σ3\thinspace\sigma (Adamson et al. 2017; Abe et al. 2018; Capozzi et al. 2018; de Salas et al. 2018a; de Salas et al. 2018b).

7.5.2 Effective number of relativistic species

New light particles appear in many extensions of the Standard Model of particle physics. Additional dark relativistic degrees of freedom are usually parameterized by NeffN_{\rm eff}, defined so that the total relativistic energy density well after electron-positron annihilation is given by

ρrad=Neff​78​(411)4/3​ργ.\rho_{\rm rad}=N_{\rm eff}\ \frac{7}{8}\left(\frac{4}{11}\right)^{4/3}\ \rho_{\gamma}. (62)

The standard cosmological model has Neff≈3.046N_{\rm eff}\approx 3.046, slightly larger than 33 since the three standard model neutrinos were not completely decoupled at electron-positron annihilation (Gnedin & Gnedin 1998; Mangano et al. 2005; de Salas & Pastor 2016).

We can treat any additional massless particles produced well before recombination (that neither interact nor decay) as simply an additional contribution to NeffN_{\rm eff}. Any species that was initially in thermal equilibrium with the Standard Model particles produces a Δ​Neff(≡Neff−3.046)\Delta N_{\rm eff}\thinspace(\equiv N_{\rm eff}-3.046) that depends only on the number of degrees of freedom and decoupling temperature. Using conservation of entropy, fully thermalized relics with gg degrees of freedom contribute

Δ​Neff=g​[434​gs]4/3×{4/7boson,1/2fermion,\Delta N_{\rm eff}=g\thinspace\left[\frac{43}{4\thinspace g_{s}}\right]^{4/3}\times\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}4/7&{\rm boson},\\ 1/2&{\rm fermion},\end{array}\right. (63)

where gsg_{s} is the effective degrees of freedom for the entropy of the other thermalized relativistic species that are present when they decouple.3838 38 For most of the thermal history gs≈g∗g_{s}\approx g_{*}, where g∗g_{*} is the effective degrees of freedom for density, but they can differ slightly, for example during the QCD phase transition (Borsanyi et al. 2016) . Examples range from a fully thermalized sterile neutrino decoupling at 1<∼T<∼1001\mathrel{\raise 1.72218pt\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{$<$\hss}\lower 5.16663pt\hbox{$\sim$}}}T\mathrel{\raise 1.72218pt\hbox{\hbox to0.0pt{$<$\hss}\lower 5.16663pt\hbox{$\sim$}}}100\thinspaceMeV, which produces Δ​Neff=1\Delta N_{\rm eff}=1, to a thermalized boson decoupling before top quark freeze-out, which produces Δ​Neff≈0.027\Delta N_{\rm eff}\approx 0.027.

Additional radiation does not need to be fully thermalized, in which case Δ​Neff\Delta N_{\rm eff} must be computed on a model-by-model basis. We follow a phenomenological approach in which we treat NeffN_{\rm eff} as a free parameter. We allow Neff<3.046N_{\rm eff}<3.046 for completeness, corresponding to standard neutrinos having a lower temperature than expected, even though such models are less well motivated theoretically.

The 2018 Planck data are still entirely consistent with Neff≈3.046N_{\rm eff}\approx 3.046, with the new low-ℓ\ell polarization constraint lowering the 2015 central value slightly and with a corresponding 10 % reduction in the error bar, giving

Neff=3.00−0.53+0.57(95 %, Planck TT+lowE),\left.N_{\rm eff}=3.00^{+0.57}_{-0.53}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT\allowbreak+lowE), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (64a)
Neff=2.92−0.37+0.36(95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE),\left.N_{\rm eff}=2.92^{+0.36}_{-0.37}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (64b)

with similar results including lensing. Modifying the relativistic energy density before recombination changes the sound horizon, which is partly degenerate with changes in the late-time geometry. Although the physical acoustic scale measured by BAO data changes in the same way, the low-redshift BAO geometry helps to partially break the degeneracies. Despite improvements in both BAO data and Planck polarization measurements, the joint Planck+BAO constraints remain similar to 284:

Neff=3.11−0.43+0.44(95 %, TT+lowE+lensing+BAO);\left.N_{\rm eff}=3.11^{+0.44}_{-0.43}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{156.49014pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO); \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (65a)
Neff=2.99−0.33+0.34(95 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO).\left.N_{\rm eff}=2.99^{+0.34}_{-0.33}\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{156.49014pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO). \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (65b)

For Neff>3.046N_{\rm eff}>3.046 the Planck data prefer higher values of the Hubble constant and fluctuation amplitude, σ8\sigma_{8}, than for the base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model. This is because higher NeffN_{\rm eff} leads to a smaller sound horizon at recombination and H0H_{0} must rise to keep the acoustic scale, θ∗=r∗/DM\theta_{*}=r_{\ast}/D_{\rm M}, fixed at the observed value. Since the change in the allowed Hubble constant with NeffN_{\rm eff} is associated with a change in the sound horizon, BAO data do not help to strongly exclude larger values of NeffN_{\rm eff}. Thus varying NeffN_{\rm eff} allows the tension with Riess et al. (2018a, R18) to be somewhat eased, as illustrated in Fig. 35. However, although the 68 % error from Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO on the Hubble parameter is weakened when allowing varying NeffN_{\rm eff}, it is still discrepant with R18 at just over 3​σ3\thinspace\sigma, giving H0=(67.3±1.1)​km​s−1​Mpc−1H_{0}=(67.3\pm 1.1)\penalty\ \text{km}\penalty\ \text{s}^{-1}\text{Mpc}^{-1}. Interpreting this discrepancy as a moderate statistical fluctuation, the combined result is

Neff=3.27±0.15H0=(69.32±0.97)​km​s−1​Mpc−1}68 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO+R18.\left.\begin{aligned} N_{\rm eff}&=3.27\pm 0.15\\ H_{0}&=(69.32\pm 0.97)\penalty\ \text{km}\penalty\ \text{s}^{-1}\text{Mpc}^{-1}\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{85.35826pt}{\begin{flushleft}68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO\allowbreak+{R18.} \end{flushleft}}}} (66)

However, as explained in 284, this set of parameters requires an increase in σ8\sigma_{8} and a decrease in Ωm\Omega_{\mathrm{m}}, potentially increasing tensions with weak galaxy lensing and (possibly) cluster count data. Higher values for NeffN_{\rm eff} also start to come into tension with observational constraints on primordial light element abundances (see Sect. 7.6).

Restricting ourselves to the more physically motivated models with Δ​Neff>0\Delta N_{\rm eff}>0, the one-tailed Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO constraint is Δ​Neff<0.30\Delta N_{\rm eff}<0.30 at 95%95\thinspace\%. This rules out light thermal relics that decoupled after the QCD phase transition (although new species are still allowed if they decoupled at higher temperatures and with gg not too large). Figure 36 shows the detailed constraint as a function of decoupling temperature, assuming only light thermal relics and other Standard Model particles.

7.5.3 Joint constraints on neutrino mass and NeffN_{\rm eff}

There are various theoretical scenarios in which it is possible to have both sterile neutrinos and neutrino mass. We first consider the case of massless relics combined with the three standard degenerate active neutrinos, varying NeffN_{\rm eff} and ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} together. The parameters are not very correlated, so the mass constraint is similar to that obtained when not also varying NeffN_{\rm eff}. We find:

Neff=2.96−0.33+0.34,∑mν<0.12​eV,}95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO.\left.\begin{aligned} N_{\rm eff}&=2.96^{+0.34}_{-0.33},\\ \sum m_{\nu}&<0.12\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV},\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO. \end{flushleft}}}} (67)

The bounds remain very close to the bounds on either NeffN_{\rm eff} (Eq. 65b) or ∑mν\sum m_{\nu} (Eq. 61b) in 7-parameter models, showing that the data clearly differentiate between the physical effects generated by the addition of these two parameters. Similar results are found without lensing and BAO data. Although the mass constraint is almost unchanged, varying NeffN_{\rm eff} does allow for larger Hubble parameters, as shown in Fig. 34. However, as discussed in 284 and the previous section, this does not substantially help to resolve possible tensions with σ8\sigma_{8} measurements from other astrophysical data.

The second case that we consider is massive sterile neutrinos combined with standard active neutrinos having a minimal-mass hierarchy, parameterizing the sterile mass by mν,sterileeff≡Ων,sterile​h2​(94.1​eV)m_{\nu,\thinspace\mathrm{sterile}}^{\mathrm{eff}}\equiv\Omega_{\nu,\rm{sterile}}h^{2}(94.1\thinspace\text{eV}) as in 276 and 284. The physical mass of the sterile neutrino in this case is msterilethermal=(ΔNeff)−3/4mν,sterileeffm_{\rm sterile}^{\rm thermal}=(\Delta N_{\rm eff})^{-3/4}m_{\nu,\thinspace\mathrm{sterile}}^{\mathrm{eff}} assuming a thermal sterile neutrino, or msterileDW=(Δ​Neff)−1​mν,sterileeffm_{\rm sterile}^{\rm DW}=(\Delta N_{\rm eff})^{-1}m_{\nu,\thinspace\mathrm{sterile}}^{\mathrm{eff}} in the case of production via the mechanism described by Dodelson & Widrow (1994). For low Δ​Neff\Delta N_{\rm eff} the physical mass can therefore become large, in which case the particles behave in the same way as cold dark matter. In our grid of parameter chains we adopt a prior that msterilethermal<10​eVm_{\rm sterile}^{\rm thermal}<10\thinspace\text{eV} (and necessarily Δ​Neff≥0\Delta N_{\rm eff}\geq 0) to exclude parameter space that is degenerate with a change in the cold dark matter density; as we show in Fig. 37, detailed constraints will depend on this choice of prior. Assuming msterilethermal<10​eVm_{\rm sterile}^{\rm thermal}<10\thinspace\text{eV} we find

Neff<3.29,mν,sterileeff<0.65​eV,}95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO,\left.\begin{aligned} N_{\rm eff}&<3.29,\\ m_{\nu,\thinspace\mathrm{sterile}}^{\mathrm{eff}}&<0.65\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV},\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO, \end{flushleft}}}} (68a)

or adopting a stronger prior of msterilethermal<2​eVm_{\rm sterile}^{\rm thermal}<2\thinspace\text{eV}, we obtain the stronger constraint

Neff<3.34,mν,sterileeff<0.23​eV,}95 %, Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO.\left.\begin{aligned} N_{\rm eff}&<3.34,\\ m_{\nu,\thinspace\mathrm{sterile}}^{\mathrm{eff}}&<0.23\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV},\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{142.26378pt}{\begin{flushleft}95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+lensing\allowbreak+BAO. \end{flushleft}}}} (68b)

The mass constraint in Eq. (68a) actually appears weaker than in 284; this is because the change in optical depth reduces the high-NeffN_{\rm eff} parameter space, and the remaining lower-NeffN_{\rm eff} parameter space has significant volume associated with models having relatively large mν,sterileeffm_{\nu,\thinspace\mathrm{sterile}}^{\mathrm{eff}} (close to the msterilethermalm_{\rm sterile}^{\rm thermal} prior cut). Removing this high-physical-mass parameter space by tightening the prior to 2​eV2\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV} gives the mass constraint in Eq. (68b), which is substantially tighter than the result quoted in 284 without high-ℓ\ell polarization.

One thermalized sterile neutrino with Δ​Neff=1\Delta N_{\rm eff}=1 is excluded at about 6​σ6\thinspace\sigma irrespective of its mass, or at about 7​σ7\thinspace\sigma when assuming a mass msterileDW≈1​eVm_{\mathrm{sterile}}^{\mathrm{DW}}\approx 1\thinspace\thinspace\text{eV}. This is especially interesting in the context of the controversial evidence for light sterile neutrinos, invoked to explain the neutrino short baseline (SBL) anomaly. The latest MiniBooNE data on electron-neutrino appearance (Aguilar-Arevalo et al. 2018) support previous anomalous results by LSND (Aguilar-Arevalo et al. 2001), with a combined significance of 6.1​σ6.1\thinspace\sigma in favour of electron-neutrino appearance. However, this contradicts recent muon-neutrino disappearance data from MINOS+ and IceCube (Dentler et al. 2018), when considered along with electron-antineutrino disappearance results (Dentler et al. 2017; Gariazzo et al. 2018), and also appears to be excluded by OPERA (Agafonova et al. 2018). The long-standing evidence for electron-neutrino disappearance in reactor experiments has also recently been challenged by new data from STEREO (Almazán et al. 2018) and PROSPECT (Ashenfelter et al. 2018). It is worth noting, however, that removing any individual experiment does not relieve the tension between the remaining experiments, and mild tension still persists if all electron (anti-)neutrino appearance (disappearance) data are removed (see Maltoni 2018, for a detailed summary). Several analyses have shown that in order to fit the anomalous data sets with one sterile neutrino, one needs an active-sterile neutrino mixing angle such that the fourth neutrino mass eigenstate would acquire a thermal distribution in the early Universe (Hannestad et al. 2013; Bridle et al. 2017; Knee et al. 2018, see e.g.,), thus contributing as Δ​Neff≈1\Delta N_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx 1. 3939 39 Note that Δ​Neff\Delta N_{\mathrm{eff}} could in principle be reduced if there was a small amount of lepton asymmetry in the early Universe; however, this would raise other types of problems (Saviano et al. 2013). Our Planck results confirm that the presence of a light thermalized sterile neutrino is in strong contradiction with cosmological data, and that the production of sterile neutrinos possibly explaining the SBL anomaly would need to be suppressed by some non-standard interactions (Archidiacono et al. 2016; Chu et al. 2015), low-temperature reheating (de Salas et al. 2015), or another special mechanism.

7.6 Big-bang nucleosynthesis

7.6.1 Primordial element abundances

Primordial helium. The latest estimates of the primordial helium abundance come from the data compilations of Aver et al. (2015), giving YPBBN≡4​nHe/nb=0.2449±0.0040Y_{\text{P}}^{\rm BBN}\equiv 4n_{\rm He}/n_{\rm b}=0.2449\pm 0.0040 (68 % CL) and Peimbert et al. (2016), giving a slightly tighter constraint YPBBN=0.2446±0.0029Y_{\text{P}}^{\rm BBN}=0.2446\pm 0.0029 (68 % CL). These two estimates are consistent with each other. Izotov et al. (2014) find a higher value, YPBBN=0.2551±0.0022Y_{\text{P}}^{\rm BBN}=0.2551\pm 0.0022 (68 % CL) in moderate (2.2σ\thinspace\sigma to 2.9σ\thinspace\sigma) tension with the previous two. Aver et al. (2015) discuss the differences between their results and Izotov et al. (2014), which are caused by modelling differences involving neutral hydrogen collisional emission, corrections for dust absorption, and helium emissivities, amongst other effects. This raises the issue, which has long-plagued helium abundance measurements, of whether the systematic errors are accurately incorporated in the quoted uncertainties. In this paper, we will use the more conservative Aver et al. (2015) results as the baseline; however, we will occasionally quote bounds based on the combined Aver et al. (2015) and Peimbert et al. (2016) results (YPBBN=0.2447±0.0023Y_{\text{P}}^{\rm BBN}=0.2447\pm 0.0023 (68 % CL)) and for the Izotov et al. (2014) results.

Compared to the measurement used in 284, the Aver et al. (2015) error bar has decreased by a factor of 2.4. To relate the primordial helium abundance to early Universe parameters under the assumption of standard BBN, we use two public BBN codes: first, version 1.10 of PArthENoPE4040 40 http://parthenope.na.infn.it. Note that PArthENoPE already exists in version 2.0, but the difference with respect to 1.10 is only at the level of numerical methods and performance. The physical input data and results are identical. (Pisanti et al. 2008); and second, the recently released PRIMAT code4141 41 http://www2.iap.fr/users/pitrou/primat.htm (Pitrou et al. 2018). The most relevant particle physics parameter for helium-abundance calculations is the neutron lifetime. PArthENoPE 1.10 uses the average value τn=(880.2±1.0)\tau_{\rm n}=(880.2\pm 1.0)\thinspaces (68 % CL) taken from the Particle Data Group summary (Patrignani et al. 2016). This is a very small shift with respect to the value of τn=(880.3±1.1)\tau_{\rm n}=(880.3\pm 1.1)\thinspaces used in 284. The PRIMAT code uses instead an average over post-2000 measurements only, τn=(879.5±0.8)\tau_{\rm n}=(879.5\pm 0.8)\thinspaces (Serebrov et al. 2018, 68 % CL,). The two codes find (consistently) that uncertainties of σ⁡(τn)=1.0\sigma(\tau_{\rm n})=1.0\thinspaces and 0.80.8\thinspaces correspond to theoretical errors for the helium fraction of σ⁡(YPBBN)=3.0×10−4\sigma(Y_{\text{P}}^{\rm BBN})=3.0\times 10^{-4} and 2.4×10−42.4\times 10^{-4}, respectively. Given the Planck result for the baryon density in the base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model,

ωb=0.02236±0.00029(95 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE),\left.\omega_{\mathrm{b}}=0.02236\pm 0.00029\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{113.81102pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (69)

PArthENoPE predicts

YPBBN=0.24672−(0.00012)​0.00061+(0.00011)​0.00061(95 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE),\left.Y_{\text{P}}^{\rm BBN}=0.24672^{+(0.00011)0.00061}_{-(0.00012)0.00061}\hskip-2.84526pt\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{102.43008pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (70a)

while PRIMAT gives

YPBBN=0.24714−(0.00013)​0.00049+(0.00012)​0.00049(95 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE).\left.Y_{\text{P}}^{\rm BBN}=0.24714^{+(0.00012)0.00049}_{-(0.00013)0.00049}\hskip-2.84526pt\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{102.43008pt}{\begin{flushleft}(95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE). \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (70b)

The first set of error bars (in parentheses) reflects only the uncertainty on ωb\omega_{\mathrm{b}}, while the second set includes the theoretical uncertainty σ⁡(YPBBN)\sigma(Y_{\text{P}}^{\rm BBN}) added in quadrature. The two mean values are shifted by Δ​YPBBN≈4.2×10−4\Delta Y_{\text{P}}^{\rm BBN}\approx 4.2\times 10^{-4} because of differences in the adopted neutron lifetime and because PRIMAT includes a more elaborate treatment of weak interaction rates. However, this shift is quite close to the theoretical errors estimated from both codes, and about an order of magnitude smaller that the observational error quoted by Aver et al. (2015). As shown in Fig. 38, the results from both codes lie well within the region favoured by the Aver et al. (2015) observations. They are also compatible at the 1σ\thinspace\sigma level with the combined Aver et al. (2015) and Peimbert et al. (2016) results, but in 3.6–3.8​σ3.8\thinspace\sigma tension with the Izotov et al. (2014) results. Evidently, there is an urgent need to resolve the differences between the helium abundance measurements and this tension should be borne in mind when we use the Aver et al. (2015) measurements below.

Primordial deuterium. There has been significant progress related to deuterium abundance determination since the completion of 284. On the observational side, Cooke et al. (2018) have published a new estimate based on their best seven measurements in metal-poor damped Ly α\alpha systems, yDP≡105​nD/nH=2.527±0.030y_{\mathrm{DP}}\equiv 10^{5}n_{\rm D}/n_{\rm H}=2.527\pm 0.030 (68 % CL). On the calculational side, the value of the nuclear reaction rate d​(p,γ)3​Hed(p,\gamma)^{3}\mbox{He}, which has a major impact on BBN computations of the primordial deuterium calculation, has now been calculated ab initio. The most recent theoretical calculation is presented in Marcucci et al. (2016, leading to a smaller value of y DP ) and differs significantly from previous predictions extrapolated from laboratory experiments by Adelberger et al. (2011). This issue should be settled by forthcoming precise measurements by the LUNA experiment (Gustavino 2017). In this paper we will compare the results obtained when the deuterium fraction is computed in three different ways:

(a)

with PArthENoPE, assuming the experimental rate from Adelberger et al. (2011);

(b)

with PArthENoPE, using the theoretical rate of Marcucci et al. (2016);

(c)

with PRIMAT, using the rate from Iliadis et al. (2016), based on a hybrid method that consists of assuming the energy dependence of the rate computed ab initio by Marcucci et al. (2005) and normalizing it with a fit to a selection of laboratory measurements.

In addition to the d​(p,γ)3​Hed(p,\gamma)^{3}\mbox{He} reaction rates, the current versions of PArthENoPE, PRIMAT, and other codes (Nollett & Burles 2000; Nollett & Holder 2011, such as that developed by) make different assumptions on other rates, in particular those of the deuterium fusion reactions d​(d,n)3d(d,n)^{3}He and d​(d,p)3d(d,p)^{3}H, which also contribute significantly to the error budget of the primordial deuterium fraction. PArthENoPE estimates these rates by averaging over all existing measurements, while PRIMAT again uses a hybrid method based on a subset of the existing data. When using one of approaches (a), (b), or (c), we adopt different theoretical errors. For (a), Adelberger et al. (2011) estimate that the error in their extrapolated rate propagates to σ⁡(yDP)=0.06\sigma(y_{\mathrm{DP}})=0.06. For (b), we rely on the claim by Marcucci et al. (2016) that the error is now dominated by uncertainties on deuterium fusion and propagates to σ⁡(yDP)=0.03\sigma(y_{\mathrm{DP}})=0.03. For (c), the error computed by PRIMAT (close to the best-fit value of ωb\omega_{\mathrm{b}}) is similar, σ⁡(yDP)=0.032\sigma(y_{\mathrm{DP}})=0.032.

These systematic error estimates are consistent with the differences between different BBN codes. Taking d​(p,γ)3​Hed(p,\gamma)^{3}\mbox{He} from Marcucci et al. (2016), the prediction of PArthENoPE 1.10 is higher than that of the code by Nollett & Holder (2011) by about Δ​yDP=0.04\Delta y_{\mathrm{DP}}=0.04, which is comparable to the theoretical error adopted in this paper. Nollett & Holder (2011) attribute this shift to their different assumptions on the deuterium fusion rates. The shift between cases (b) and (c) is smaller, Δ​yDP=0.015\Delta y_{\mathrm{DP}}=0.015, suggesting that differences in d​(p,γ)3​Hed(p,\gamma)^{3}\mbox{He} and in the deuterium fusion rates nearly compensate each other in the final result.

Nuclear rate uncertainties are critically important in the discussion of the compatibility between deuterium measurements and CMB data. Cooke et al. (2018) reported that their measurement of primordial deuterium was in moderate 2.0σ\thinspace\sigma tension with the Planck baryon density from 284. This is based on the predictions of the code of Nollett & Holder (2011) with the nuclear rate of Marcucci et al. (2016). Switching to PArthENoPE (b) and including the theoretical error σ⁡(yDP)=0.03\sigma(y_{\mathrm{DP}})=0.03, we find consistency to 1.1σ\thinspace\sigma. With our three BBN calculation pipelines, the deuterium abundance measurement of Cooke et al. (2018) translates into the following bounds on ωb\omega_{\mathrm{b}},

(a)​ωb=0.02270±0.00075(b)​ωb=0.02198±0.00044(c)​ωb=0.02189±0.00046}   95 %,  Cooke (2018),  \left.\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{(a)\ }\thinspace\thinspace\omega_{\mathrm{b}}=0.02270\pm 0.00075\\ &\mathrm{(b)\ }\thinspace\thinspace\omega_{\mathrm{b}}=0.02198\pm 0.00044\\ &\mathrm{(c)\ }\thinspace\thinspace\omega_{\mathrm{b}}=0.02189\pm 0.00046\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{113.81102pt}{\begin{flushleft}95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ \\ Cooke\penalty\ (2018), \end{flushleft}}}} (71)

including theoretical errors. In several places in this work and in 294, we refer to a “conservative BBN prior,” ωb=0.0222±0.0005\omega_{\mathrm{b}}=0.0222\pm 0.0005 (68% CL), set to be compatible with each of these three predictions.

We now update this discussion using the latest Planck results. With our three assumptions (a), (b), and (c) on standard BBN, the determination of ωb\omega_{\mathrm{b}} by Planck 2018 for the base-Λ\LambdaCDM model (see Eq. 69) implies

(a)​yDP=2.587−(0.052)​0.13+(0.055)​0.13(b)​yDP=2.455−(0.053)​0.080+(0.054)​0.081(c)​yDP=2.439−(0.051)​0.081+(0.053)​0.082}95 %, TT,TE,EE+lowE,\left.\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{(a)\ }\thinspace\thinspace y_{\mathrm{DP}}=2.587^{+(0.055)0.13}_{-(0.052)0.13}\\ &\mathrm{(b)\ }\thinspace\thinspace y_{\mathrm{DP}}=2.455^{+(0.054)0.081}_{-(0.053)0.080}\\ &\mathrm{(c)\ }\thinspace\thinspace y_{\mathrm{DP}}=2.439^{+(0.053)0.082}_{-(0.051)0.081}\end{aligned}\ \right\}\ \ \mbox{\text{\parbox{113.81102pt}{\begin{flushleft}95\thinspace\%,\penalty\ TT,TE,EE\allowbreak+lowE, \end{flushleft}}}} (72)

with the ωb\omega_{\mathrm{b}}-only error between parentheses, followed by the total error including the theoretical uncertainty. These results are in agreement with the Cooke et al. (2018) measurement to within 0.8σ\thinspace\sigma, 1.4σ\thinspace\sigma, and 1.7σ\thinspace\sigma, respectively. Thus no significant tensions are found in any of these cases.

Other light elements. We do not discuss other light elements, such as tritium and lithium, since the observed abundance measurements and their interpretation in terms of the standard models of BBN are more controversial (see Fields 2011; Fields et al. 2014, for reviews). The Planck results do not shed any further light on these problems compared to earlier CMB experiments.

Nuclear rates from bounds from Planck. The previous paragraphs highlighted the importance of assumptions on the radiative-capture process d​(p,γ)3​He{\rm d}({\rm p},\gamma)^{3}\mbox{He} for deuterium abundance predictions. It is worth checking whether the comparison of CMB and deuterium abundance data provides an indirect estimate of this rate. This approach was suggested in Cooke et al. (2014) and implemented in Di Valentino et al. (2014) and 284. We can now update it using the latest Planck and deuterium data.

We parameterize the thermal rate R2​(T)R_{2}(T) of the d​(p,γ)3​He{\rm d}({\rm p},\gamma)^{3}\mbox{He} process in the PArthENoPE code by rescaling the rate R2ex​(T)R_{2}^{\rm ex}(T) fitted to experimental data by Adelberger et al. (2011) with a factor A2A_{2}:

R2​(T)=A2​R2ex​(T).R_{2}(T)=A_{2}\thinspace R_{2}^{\rm ex}(T)\thinspace. (73)

This factor does not account in an exact way for the differences between the experimental fit and the theoretical predictions; it should instead be seen as a consistency parameter, very much like ALA_{\rm L} for CMB lensing in Sect. 6.2. The rate R2th​(T)R_{2}^{\rm th}(T) predicted by Marcucci et al. (2005) has a temperature dependence that is close to what is measured experimentally, and can be very well approximated by a rescaling factor A2=1.055A_{2}=1.055. The new theoretical rate obtained by Marcucci et al. (2016) has a slightly different temperature dependence but is well approximated by an effective rescaling factor A2th=1.16A_{2}^{\rm th}=1.16 (Mangano & Pisanti, private communication).

Assuming the base-Λ​CDM\rm{\Lambda CDM} model, we then constrain A2A_{2} using Planck data combined with the latest deuterium abundance measurements from Cooke et al. (2018). We still need to take into account theoretical errors on deuterium predictions arising from uncertainties on other rates, and from the difference between various codes. According to Marcucci et al. (2016) and Pitrou et al. Thus we adopt σ⁡(yDP)=0.03\sigma(y_{\rm DP})=0.03 as the theoretical error on deuterium predictions in this analysis. Adding the theoretical error in quadrature to the observational error of Cooke et al. (2018), we obtain a total error of σ⁡(yDP)=0.042\sigma(y_{\rm DP})=0.042 on deuterium, which we use in our joint fits of Planck+deutrium (D) data. We find

A2=1.138±0.072(68 %, Planck TT+lowE+D),\left.A_{2}=1.138\pm 0.072\quad\mbox{\text{\parbox{119.50148pt}{\begin{flushleft}(68\thinspace\%,\penalty\ {Planck}\ TT\allowbreak+lowE\allowbreak+{\rm D}), \end{flushleft}}}}\right. (74a)
